chapters.title: Organic Chemistry
chapters.summary: This chapter introduces organic chemistry through the study of fossil fuels—petroleum, coal, and natural gas. It explains how these fuels formed from ancient organisms and examines the hydrocarbons and organic compounds they contain.

book_skeleton.subject_overview: This textbook introduces organic chemistry, focusing on fossil fuels and hydrocarbons. It explains the composition of petroleum, coal, and natural gas, and describes the carbon-based organic compounds that make up these fossil fuels.

chapters.title: Organic Chemistry
chapters.summary: This chapter introduces organic chemistry through the study of fossil fuels—petroleum, coal, and natural gas. It explains how these fuels formed from ancient organisms and examines the hydrocarbons and organic compounds they contain.

events.text: C = carbon, H = hydrogen
Petroleum = a mixture of hydrocarbons (carbon + hydrogen)
Crude oil = mixture of many hydrocarbons
Small molecules boil first (low temp); big molecules need high temp
Vapour condenses where it cools to its boiling point
Q: Refine petroleum by collecting fractions as the thermometer rises
Smaller lighter molecules evaporate first - swap first test-tube at 100 degrees Celsius
Swap again at 150, 200, and 300 degrees Celsius
Four fractions collected total, at 100, 150, 200, and 300 degrees Celsius
Q: How do the four fractions compare in boiling point, runniness, volatility, and flammability?
Fraction 1: bp up to 100 C, very runny, volatile, burns very easily, small molecules
Fraction 2: bp 100 to 150 C, runny, less volatile, burns easily
Fraction 3: bp 150 to 200 C, not very runny, even less volatile, not easily burns
Fraction 4: bp 200 to 300 C, viscous, least volatile, burns only with a wick, large molecules
As molecules get larger (Fraction 1 to 4), boiling point rises; runniness, volatility, and flammability all decrease.
Q: Name each refinery fraction by its carbon range and its use.
Refinery gas: C1 to C4, cooking and heating gas
Gasoline (petrol): C5 to C6, car fuel
Naphtha: C6 to C10, chemicals and plastics feedstock
Paraffin (kerosene): C10 to C15, aircraft and lamp fuel
Diesel oil: C15 to C20, diesel engine fuel
Fuel oil: C20 to C30, power stations and ships
Lubricating fraction: C30 to C50, engine oil and waxes
Bitumen: C50 upwards, road surfaces and roofs
Eight fractions: refinery gas (C1-C4) to bitumen (C50+), heaviest at the hot base, lightest at the cool top
Fractional distillation sorts crude oil into fractions by boiling point
Cracking = breaking large hydrocarbons into smaller, more useful ones
alkene = has a C=C double bond
Cracking makes an alkane AND an alkene; the alkene builds plastics
Q: Crack decane (C10H22) from naphtha at 540 C with a catalyst
Reactant: C10H22 (10 carbons, 22 hydrogens)
Products: C5H12 + C3H6 + C2H4
Carbons: 5+3+2 = 10. Hydrogens: 12+6+4 = 22.
Propene and ethene are alkenes with C=C double bonds, very reactive
Q: Crack ethane using steam at over 800 degrees Celsius. What forms?
Ethane, with steam at greater than 800 degrees Celsius, gives ethene plus hydrogen (H2)
Products: ethene + hydrogen (H2); the hydrogen can be used to make ammonia
Q: What does the gas fraction separate into?
methane, ethane, propane, butane (butane sold in canisters)
prefix = carbon count
Name = (how many carbons) + (which family)
Q: Use the general formula CnH2n+2 to find the formulas of methane, ethane, and propane
Methane: n = 1, so C1H(2x1+2) = CH4
Ethane: n = 2, so C2H(2x2+2) = C2H6
Propane: n = 3, so C3H(2x3+2) = C3H8
Methane CH4, Ethane C2H6, Propane C3H8
Q: How does boiling point change from methane to butane?
Methane (1 C): about -164 degrees C
Ethane (2 C): higher than methane
Propane (3 C): about -42 degrees C
Butane (4 C): about -0.5 degrees C
Boiling point increases as chain length increases (methane < ethane < propane < butane)
Hydrocarbon = carbon + hydrogen only
Every C-C bond is single, so alkanes are saturated
Each step: +1 carbon, +2 hydrogens
Q: What is the complete combustion of methane?
Reactants: one C H four plus two O two
Q: Write the incomplete combustion of methane in insufficient oxygen
Products: 2 CO + 4 H2O + less heat
Q: What happens when methane reacts with chlorine in sunlight?
CH3Cl, then CH2Cl2, then CHCl3, then CCl4
Q: Butane and 2-methylpropane both have formula C4H10. Compare their boiling points.
Butane (straight chain): boiling point = 0 degrees Celsius
2-methylpropane (branched): boiling point = -10 degrees Celsius
Branched isomer has the lower boiling point
Branched 2-methylpropane boils lower (-10 degrees Celsius vs 0 degrees Celsius for butane), because branching reduces attraction between molecules.
Ten carbons: 2 times 10 plus 2 = 22 hydrogens
Every alkene has a C=C double bond, its functional group
C=C present means unsaturated
Alkenes: C n H 2 n
Every alkene fits C-n-H-2-n because the double bond costs one pair of hydrogens
double bond opens, atoms add on
Q: Crack ethane with steam at over 800 C — what forms?
ethane + steam, over 800 C → cracking
ethane → ethene + hydrogen
Q: What does ethene form when it reacts with hydrogen?
Ethene (gas) + hydrogen gas, with a catalyst, heat and pressure
Q: What does ethene form when it adds water across its double bond?
Ethene (gas) plus water as steam, with a catalyst, heat and pressure
The product is ethanol, a liquid alcohol
Q: Many ethene monomers join by polymerisation — what forms?
Step 1: Many ethene monomers (the monomer) join by polymerisation.
Product = poly(ethene) / polythene — chains many thousands of carbon atoms long.
Q: What happens when ethene gas is bubbled through orange bromine water?
ethene (gas) + bromine water (orange) gives an addition reaction
ethene + bromine water gives 1,2-dibromoethane (colourless) — the orange colour disappears
Q: Three compounds all have formula C4H8 but different structures. What are they?
The three C4H8 isomers are but-1-ene, but-2-ene and 2-methylpropene
O-H group on a carbon chain = alcohol

events.title: One pattern for the whole family

events.text: General formula: C n H two n plus one O H
Q: How is ethanol made from glucose by fermentation?
Q: How is ethanol made by hydration of ethene?
Conditions: 570 degrees C, 60-70 atm, phosphoric acid catalyst
Q: Combustion of ethanol in oxygen
same O-H group = similar reactions
C-O-O-H = the carboxyl group
chain grows, carboxyl group stays
General formula C n H two n O two
Q: Show how the boiling points of the carboxylic acids change as the molecules get bigger.
Methanoic acid, 1 carbon, boiling point 101 degrees Celsius
Ethanoic acid, 2 carbons, boiling point 118 degrees Celsius
Propanoic acid, 3 carbons, boiling point 141 degrees Celsius
Butanoic acid, 4 carbons, boiling point 164 degrees Celsius
Boiling points rise with size: 101, 118, 141, 164 degrees Celsius for 1 to 4 carbons
Q: Oxidise ethanol to ethanoic acid using potassium manganate(VII) in acid — what is the colour change?
Acid provides H+ ions for the reaction
Potassium manganate(VII): purple → colourless. Alternative — potassium dichromate(VI): orange → green.
Q: Why is ethanoic acid a weak acid?
Ethanoic acid is a weak acid because only some of its molecules dissociate into ethanoate ions and hydrogen ions.
Q: What happens when ethanoic acid reacts with sodium hydroxide?
Products: sodium ethanoate (the salt, an ionic compound) + water
Q: Ethanoic acid + propanol, with conc. sulfuric acid — what forms?
ethanoic acid + propanol → propyl ethanoate + water
Propyl ethanoate (an ester, smells of pears) + water; reversible, sulfuric acid catalyst

chapters.narration_text:
<<TOPIC_START:topic:chemistry:organic_chemistry:17_1>>
The petrol burning in a car engine today was once living creatures, swimming in an ocean millions of years ago, long before the dinosaurs. <<SECTION:Fossil fuels|id=sec-1>> When those tiny organisms died, they sank to the sea floor and got buried under thick layers of sediment, deeper and deeper, year after year. Then, over millions of years, enormous pressure and heat slowly squeezed and cooked those buried remains into something new entirely. <<PAUSE:short>> That something is petroleum, also called crude oil — and along with coal and natural gas, it is what we call a fossil fuel, because it really is made from ancient fossils. <<PAUSE:short>> But here is the strange part: if you could smell a drop of crude oil, you would be smelling not one substance, but hundreds of different compounds all mixed together. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:organic_chemistry:17_1:hydrocarbon_skeletons>> <<SECTION:Hydrocarbons|id=sec-2>> So what are all these compounds made of? Almost all of them are built from just two kinds of atom — carbon and hydrogen — and <<FOCUS:carbon-chain>> we call those molecules hydrocarbons. <<PAUSE:short>> Watch this chain take shape. <<FOCUS:carbon-atom-label>> Each grey atom here is carbon, the backbone of the whole molecule. <<WRITE_TEXT:C = carbon, H = hydrogen|id=text-1>> This carbon, marked C, links to its neighbours, and every spare arm <<FOCUS:hydrogen-atom-label>> grabs a hydrogen atom, marked H. <<UNFOCUS>> Carbon and hydrogen — that is the whole recipe. <<PAUSE:short>> Now, why hundreds of different compounds? Because carbon is a master builder — the same atoms can connect <<FOCUS:carbon-chain>> in a straight chain, or <<FOCUS:carbon-ring>> curl right around into a ring. <<UNFOCUS>> Short chains, long chains, rings, branches — each different shape is a different compound, which is exactly why crude oil is such a rich mixture. <<WRITE_KEY:Petroleum = a mixture of hydrocarbons (carbon + hydrogen)|id=key-1>> So remember this: petroleum is not one chemical, it is a mixture of hydrocarbons, molecules made only from carbon and hydrogen. <<PAUSE:short>> And every time you fill a tank, you are burning carbon chains that took an ocean, a graveyard of ancient life, and millions of years of pressure to build.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:chemistry:organic_chemistry:17_2>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:organic_chemistry:17_2:distillation_column>> Pump crude oil out of the ground and you don't get fuel — you get a <<FOCUS:crude-oil-flask>> thick black soup of hundreds of different molecules, all jumbled together. Every one of those molecules is a hydrocarbon — built only from hydrogen and carbon — but they come in wildly different sizes, <<FOCUS:small-molecule+large-molecule>> from tiny short chains to enormous long ones. <<WRITE_TEXT:Crude oil = mixture of many hydrocarbons|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> A giant jumbled mixture like this is almost useless, so our first job is to sort it — and the trick is hiding in how these molecules behave when you heat them. Here's the question: if I <<FOCUS:heat-source>> gently warm this whole mixture, which molecules do you think escape the liquid first? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The small, light ones. They're loosely held, so it takes only a little energy to free them — <<FOCUS:small-molecule>> they boil off first, at low temperatures. The <<FOCUS:large-molecule>> big heavy molecules cling on and need far more heat to escape. <<WRITE_KEY:Small molecules boil first (low temp); big molecules need high temp|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> So we heat the crude oil and <<TRACE:rising-vapour>> let the vapours rise up through a tall column that's <<FOCUS:temp-bot-label+temp-top-label>> hot at the bottom and cool at the top. <<UNFOCUS>> As a vapour climbs and cools, it condenses back into a liquid the moment it reaches its own boiling temperature — and we collect it there. <<WRITE_TEXT:Vapour condenses where it cools to its boiling point|id=text-2>> The lightest molecules stay as gas highest up and are <<FOCUS:fraction-light>> caught at the cool top of the column. The heaviest molecules barely rise at all — they condense low down where it's still scorching hot, and are <<FOCUS:fraction-heavy>> drawn off at the bottom. <<SECTION:The fractions|id=sec-2>> Because the lighter molecules boil at lower temperatures, <<FOCUS:column>> each height in the column traps molecules of one particular size — that's exactly why the sorting works. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter: refining petroleum in the lab. We gently heat the petroleum and let the compounds evaporate, collecting what condenses in cool test-tubes. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Refine petroleum by collecting fractions as the thermometer rises|id=ex-q-1>> We start by watching what evaporates first. The smaller, lighter molecules go first, since it takes less energy to free them from the liquid. As the hot vapours rise, so does the thermometer reading. When the reading reaches one hundred degrees Celsius, we swap the first test-tube for an empty one, and that liquid is our first fraction. <<WRITE_STEP:Smaller lighter molecules evaporate first - swap first test-tube at 100 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-1>> Then we collect three more fractions in the same way, swapping the test-tube at one hundred and fifty degrees Celsius, at two hundred degrees Celsius, and at three hundred degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Swap again at 150, 200, and 300 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-2>> And the answer is that we end up with four fractions collected in total, each gathered over a rising temperature range. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Four fractions collected total, at 100, 150, 200, and 300 degrees Celsius|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We're comparing four fractions collected from distillation, and we want to see how their properties change as the molecules get larger. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How do the four fractions compare in boiling point, runniness, volatility, and flammability?|id=ex-q-1>> Let's lay them out in order. Fraction one boils up to one hundred degrees Celsius, it's very runny, very volatile, burns very easily, and it's made of small molecules. <<WRITE_STEP:Fraction 1: bp up to 100 C, very runny, volatile, burns very easily, small molecules|id=ex-step-1-1>> Fraction two boils between one hundred and one hundred fifty degrees Celsius, it's runny, less volatile, and burns easily. <<WRITE_STEP:Fraction 2: bp 100 to 150 C, runny, less volatile, burns easily|id=ex-step-1-2>> Continuing down, fraction three boils between one hundred fifty and two hundred degrees Celsius, it's not very runny, even less volatile, and it does not burn easily. <<WRITE_STEP:Fraction 3: bp 150 to 200 C, not very runny, even less volatile, not easily burns|id=ex-step-1-3>> And fraction four boils between two hundred and three hundred degrees Celsius, it's viscous, thick and sticky, the least volatile, it only burns with a wick, and it's made of large molecules. <<WRITE_STEP:Fraction 4: bp 200 to 300 C, viscous, least volatile, burns only with a wick, large molecules|id=ex-step-1-4>> So the pattern is clear: as the molecules get larger from fraction one through fraction four, the boiling point rises while runniness, volatility, and flammability all decrease together. <<WRITE_ANSWER:As molecules get larger (Fraction 1 to 4), boiling point rises; runniness, volatility, and flammability all decrease.|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. A fractional distillation tower separates crude oil by the size of the molecules. At the base it's over four hundred degrees Celsius, and near the top it's about twenty-five degrees Celsius. The bigger molecules condense low down where it's hot, and the smaller ones rise to the cooler top. Let's list the fractions from lightest to heaviest. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Name each refinery fraction by its carbon range and its use.|id=ex-q-1>> We start at the top of the tower with the smallest molecules. Refinery gas has one to four carbon atoms and is used as bottled gas for cooking and heating. <<WRITE_STEP:Refinery gas: C1 to C4, cooking and heating gas|id=ex-step-1-1>> Next is gasoline, or petrol, with five to six carbon atoms, used as fuel for cars. <<WRITE_STEP:Gasoline (petrol): C5 to C6, car fuel|id=ex-step-1-2>> Then naphtha, six to ten carbon atoms, the feedstock for many chemicals and plastics. <<WRITE_STEP:Naphtha: C6 to C10, chemicals and plastics feedstock|id=ex-step-1-3>> Moving down where it's warmer, paraffin, also called kerosene, has ten to fifteen carbon atoms and fuels aircraft and lamps. <<WRITE_STEP:Paraffin (kerosene): C10 to C15, aircraft and lamp fuel|id=ex-step-1-4>> Diesel oil has fifteen to twenty carbon atoms for diesel engines. <<WRITE_STEP:Diesel oil: C15 to C20, diesel engine fuel|id=ex-step-1-5>> Fuel oil has twenty to thirty carbon atoms for power stations and ships. <<WRITE_STEP:Fuel oil: C20 to C30, power stations and ships|id=ex-step-1-6>> Finally, at the hot base of the tower, the heaviest molecules. The lubricating fraction has thirty to fifty carbon atoms, giving engine oil and waxes. <<WRITE_STEP:Lubricating fraction: C30 to C50, engine oil and waxes|id=ex-step-1-7>> And bitumen, with fifty carbon atoms upwards, is used for road surfaces and roofs. <<WRITE_STEP:Bitumen: C50 upwards, road surfaces and roofs|id=ex-step-1-8>> So the full set of fractions, from refinery gas at one to four carbon atoms up top, down to bitumen at fifty carbons and beyond at the base. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Eight fractions: refinery gas (C1-C4) to bitumen (C50+), heaviest at the hot base, lightest at the cool top|id=ex-ans-1>> This whole process of separating crude oil into groups of similar-sized molecules has a name: fractional distillation, and the groups we collect are called fractions. <<WRITE_KEY:Fractional distillation sorts crude oil into fractions by boiling point|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> And that's the magic: one black useless soup goes in, and out come neat fractions — from runny, easily-burning fuels at the top to thick, heavy oils at the bottom — each one sorted purely by how easily its molecules let go of the liquid. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:chemistry:organic_chemistry:17_3>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:organic_chemistry:17_3:cracking_split>> Crude oil gives us far too much thick, heavy gloop that nobody wants, and never enough of the light petrol everyone is desperate for. So how do we turn the useless into the valuable? <<SECTION:Cracking|id=sec-1>> Here is the heavy stuff: <<FOCUS:long-chain>> a hydrocarbon with a long chain of carbon atoms. <<UNFOCUS>> Long chains mean a high boiling point, hard to set alight, not much use as a fuel. <<PAUSE:short>> Now imagine heating it really hard, and passing it over a hot catalyst. Something has to give. Where do you think <<FOCUS:break-point>> this long chain will break? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Cracking = breaking large hydrocarbons into smaller, more useful ones|id=key-1>> It snaps in the middle. The chain breaks <<FOCUS:small-alkane+small-alkene>> into two smaller pieces, and that is cracking: breaking big molecules into smaller, more useful ones. <<PAUSE:short>> On this side we get <<FOCUS:small-alkane>> a short chain where every carbon already holds all the hydrogen it can. <<UNFOCUS>> We call that an alkane, and it is exactly the smaller, lighter fuel we wanted. But here is the catch. When the chain snapped, <<FOCUS:small-alkene>> this other piece was left short of hydrogen. <<UNFOCUS>> Two of its carbons grab each other extra tightly instead. <<WRITE_TEXT:alkene = has a C=C double bond|id=text-1>> That extra-tight grip is <<FOCUS:double-bond>> a double bond between two carbon atoms. <<UNFOCUS>> A molecule with a carbon-to-carbon double bond is called an alkene. Why should anyone care about that double bond? It looks like a small detail on the picture. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Cracking makes an alkane AND an alkene; the alkene builds plastics|id=key-2>> Because <<FOCUS:double-bond>> that double bond is hungry to react. <<UNFOCUS>> It lets thousands of alkene molecules link up into long chains, and those long chains are plastics. No cracking, no plastic. <<PAUSE:short>> So one big useless molecule becomes two prizes at once: a useful small fuel, and a reactive alkene for making materials. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter. We take decane, with the formula C ten H twenty-two, which comes from the naphtha fraction. We heat it to five hundred and forty degrees Celsius with a catalyst, and it cracks into smaller molecules. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Crack decane (C10H22) from naphtha at 540 C with a catalyst|id=ex-q-1>> One large hydrocarbon breaks down into one smaller alkane plus one alkene, and every atom is conserved. <<WRITE_EQUATION:C_{10}H_{22} \rightarrow C_{8}H_{18} + C_{2}H_{4}|id=eq-1|boxed>> We start by writing the reactant. One molecule of decane, C ten H twenty-two, contains ten carbon atoms and twenty-two hydrogen atoms. <<WRITE_STEP:Reactant: C10H22 (10 carbons, 22 hydrogens)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now we break it into three smaller molecules. It gives pentane, C five H twelve, which is suitable for petrol, plus propene, C three H six, plus ethene, C two H four. <<WRITE_STEP:Products: C5H12 + C3H6 + C2H4|id=ex-step-1-2>> Let's check the atoms balance. On the product side the carbons are five plus three plus two, which makes ten carbons, matching the decane. The hydrogens are twelve plus six plus four, which makes twenty-two hydrogens, again matching. So ten carbons and twenty-two hydrogens split cleanly into three molecules. <<WRITE_STEP:Carbons: 5+3+2 = 10. Hydrogens: 12+6+4 = 22.|id=ex-step-1-3>> Notice that propene and ethene each contain a carbon-to-carbon double bond. They belong to the alkene family, and that double bond makes them very reactive. <<WRITE_STEP:Propene and ethene are alkenes with C=C double bonds, very reactive|id=ex-step-1-4>> And the answer is that decane has been broken down into three smaller molecules: pentane, suitable for petrol, plus the reactive alkenes propene and ethene. <<WRITE_ANSWER:C10H22 -> C5H12 + C3H6 + C2H4|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Ethane has very short molecules, but even it can be cracked. We take ethane and pass it with steam at greater than eight hundred degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Crack ethane using steam at over 800 degrees Celsius. What forms?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by breaking the ethane molecule apart under those harsh conditions. Cracking always pulls out a small reactive piece, leaving behind a molecule with a double bond. So ethane splits to give ethene plus hydrogen, that is, H two. <<WRITE_STEP:Ethane, with steam at greater than 800 degrees Celsius, gives ethene plus hydrogen (H2)|id=ex-step-1-1>> And the answer is ethene and hydrogen. Notice we get that reactive double-bonded product, ethene, and the hydrogen produced can be used to make ammonia. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Products: ethene + hydrogen (H2); the hydrogen can be used to make ammonia|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. After crude oil is fractionally distilled, some of the fractions are still mixtures, so they get split further into individual compounds. Take the gas fraction as our case. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What does the gas fraction separate into?|id=ex-q-1>> The gas fraction is separated into four individual compounds: methane, ethane, propane, and butane. <<WRITE_STEP:Gas fraction -> methane, ethane, propane, butane|id=ex-step-1-1>> And here's the everyday connection: butane is the one we buy in canisters. So the gas fraction yields methane, ethane, propane, and butane, with butane sold in canisters. <<WRITE_ANSWER:methane, ethane, propane, butane (butane sold in canisters)|id=ex-ans-1>> And because heat alone tore that strong molecule apart, chemists give cracking its proper name: thermal decomposition, breaking down using heat. <<WRITE_EQUATION:C_{10}H_{22} \rightarrow C_{8}H_{18} + C_{2}H_{4}|id=eq-1>> In symbols, one large hydrocarbon arrow gives one smaller alkane plus one alkene. Count the atoms on each side and you will see nothing is lost, just rearranged.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:chemistry:organic_chemistry:17_4>>
There are more than ten million known organic compounds — and yet you will never have to memorize a single one of their names, because every name is secretly a code. Here is the trick that chemists worked out: instead of inventing a random name for each compound, they built the name out of two clues stuck together. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:organic_chemistry:17_4:name_decoder>> <<SECTION:The hidden code|id=sec-1>> Look at this name on the board — <<FOCUS:full-name>> propanol. It looks like one word, but it is <<FOCUS:split-line>> really two pieces of information glued together. The ending of the name — <<FOCUS:suffix-part>> the very last part — tells you which family the compound belongs to. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> If a name ends in -ane it is an alkane, if it ends in -ene it is an alkene, if it ends in -ol it is an alcohol, and if it ends in -oic acid it is a carboxylic acid. <<PAUSE:short>> So <<FOCUS:suffix-part>> this ending, -ol, immediately tells me: this compound is a member of <<FOCUS:family-tag>> the alcohol family. <<UNFOCUS>> I did not have to look anything up. Now, the family alone is not enough — alcohols come in many sizes. So what tells me how big this particular molecule is? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:prefix-part>> The beginning of the name carries that second clue. <<WRITE_TEXT:prefix = carbon count|id=text-1>> The prefix tells you exactly <<FOCUS:carbon-chain>> how many carbon atoms are in the chain. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Meth- means one carbon, eth- means two, prop- means three, and but- means four. So prop- tells me this molecule has exactly <<FOCUS:carbon-count-label>> three carbon atoms. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Name = (how many carbons) + (which family)|id=key-1>> Put the two clues together and the name decodes itself: <<FOCUS:prefix-part+suffix-part>> prop plus ol means a three-carbon molecule in the alcohol family. <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. For the alkanes, the general formula is C n H two n plus two, where n is just a number that tells you how many carbon atoms are in the molecule. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Use the general formula CnH2n+2 to find the formulas of methane, ethane, and propane|id=ex-q-1>> Let's start with methane. For methane, n is one. So we put one in for n, and two times one plus two gives four hydrogens. That's C one H four, which we write as CH four. <<WRITE_STEP:Methane: n = 1, so C1H(2x1+2) = CH4|id=ex-step-1-1>> Next, ethane. For ethane, n is two. Two carbons, and two times two plus two gives six hydrogens. So that's C two H six. <<WRITE_STEP:Ethane: n = 2, so C2H(2x2+2) = C2H6|id=ex-step-1-2>> And finally propane. For propane, n is three. Three carbons, and two times three plus two gives eight hydrogens. So that's C three H eight. <<WRITE_STEP:Propane: n = 3, so C3H(2x3+2) = C3H8|id=ex-step-1-3>> And there are our answers: methane is CH four, ethane is C two H six, and propane is C three H eight, all built straight from the general formula C n H two n plus two. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Methane CH4, Ethane C2H6, Propane C3H8|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Let's look at the first four members of the alkane family and watch what happens to their boiling points. Methane has one carbon atom, ethane has two carbon atoms, propane has three carbon atoms, and butane has four carbon atoms. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How does boiling point change from methane to butane?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by listing each one with its boiling point. Methane, with just one carbon, has the lowest boiling point at about minus one hundred sixty-four degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Methane (1 C): about -164 degrees C|id=ex-step-1-1>> Ethane, with two carbons, boils a little higher. <<WRITE_STEP:Ethane (2 C): higher than methane|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now we keep going up the chain. Propane, with three carbons, boils at about minus forty-two degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Propane (3 C): about -42 degrees C|id=ex-step-1-3>> And butane, with four carbons, boils at about minus zero point five degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Butane (4 C): about -0.5 degrees C|id=ex-step-1-4>> Look at the pattern: each time we add a carbon, the boiling point climbs. So the answer is clear, the boiling point increases as the chain length increases. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Boiling point increases as chain length increases (methane < ethane < propane < butane)|id=ex-ans-1>> And the simplest family of all, the alkanes, shows the pattern beautifully: methane has one carbon, ethane two, propane three, butane four — and as the chains get longer, the boiling points climb steadily upward. So once you know the endings and the beginnings, you have not learned one compound — you have learned how to read millions of them at a glance.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:chemistry:organic_chemistry:17_5>>
The gas that cooks your dinner, the fuel in a camping stove, the stuff inside a cigarette lighter, they all come from one single family of molecules built from just two ingredients. <<SECTION:The Alkanes|id=sec-1>> Those two ingredients are carbon and hydrogen, and a molecule made of only carbon and hydrogen has a special name, a hydrocarbon. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:organic_chemistry:17_5:ethane_bonding>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Hydrocarbon = carbon + hydrogen only|id=text-1>> The alkanes are the simplest hydrocarbons of all, and the cleanest way to meet them is to look at one molecule up close. Now look right at the middle, at <<FOCUS:cc-bond>> the link joining the two carbons together. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> That link is one shared pair of electrons, and one shared pair is exactly what we mean by a single bond. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Every C-C bond is single, so alkanes are saturated|id=key-1>> And this is the rule for the whole family: every carbon-to-carbon bond is a single bond, with no spare bonds left over, which is why we call the alkanes saturated. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:A family with a pattern|id=sec-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> The alkanes aren't just one molecule though, they're a whole series, and the series follows a beautifully simple pattern. Start with methane, one carbon. Add a carbon and two hydrogens and you get ethane. Add another carbon and two more hydrogens and you get propane. So if I just told you a molecule has ten carbons, could you tell me exactly how many hydrogens it must have, without ever seeing it? <<PAUSE:long>> Because each member differs from the next by one carbon and two hydrogens, the number of hydrogens is always two times the number of carbons, plus two more. <<WRITE_EQUATION:C_nH_{2n+2}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Each step: +1 carbon, +2 hydrogens|id=key-2>> Yes, you can, because each member differs from the next by one carbon and two hydrogens, and that locks in the formula carbon-n hydrogen two-n-plus-two. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter. When methane burns in a good supply of oxygen, it undergoes complete combustion. We start with one molecule of methane, that's C H four, reacting with two molecules of oxygen, two O two. The reaction needs that good supply of oxygen to burn cleanly. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What is the complete combustion of methane?|id=ex-q-1>> Now we write the reactants on the left. One methane molecule plus two oxygen molecules. <<WRITE_STEP:Reactants: one C H four plus two O two|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow|id=ex-eq-1>> These react together to form the products. One molecule of methane gives one carbon dioxide, that's one C O two, plus two molecules of water, two H two O, and it releases plenty of heat energy. So the answer is: C H four plus two O two gives one C O two plus two H two O plus heat energy. <<WRITE_ANSWER:CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O + heat energy|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. When there isn't enough oxygen, alkanes undergo incomplete combustion, and instead of carbon dioxide they produce poisonous carbon monoxide. Let's balance the equation for methane burning in too little oxygen. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Write the incomplete combustion of methane in insufficient oxygen|id=ex-q-1>> We start on the left side with two molecules of methane reacting with three molecules of oxygen. Because there isn't enough oxygen, the carbon can't fully oxidise. <<WRITE_STEP:2 CH4 + 3 O2 -> ?|id=ex-step-1-1>> Working out the products: the carbon ends up as carbon monoxide, so we get two molecules of carbon monoxide, and the hydrogen forms four molecules of water. Methane reacts with chlorine, that's C-l-two, but only in sunlight. In sunlight, methane plus chlorine produces chloromethane, C-H-three-C-l, plus hydrogen chloride, H-C-l. But how do all the members of this family relate to one another? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> They form a homologous series, which is just a fancy name for a family where each member follows the same pattern and differs from the next by a fixed building block. <<SECTION:The general formula|id=sec-2>> And that pattern is beautifully simple. In every alkene, the number of hydrogen atoms is always exactly <<FOCUS:hydrogen-atoms+carbon-left+carbon-right>> twice the number of carbon atoms. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The number of hydrogen atoms is always exactly twice the number of carbon atoms. <<WRITE_EQUATION:C_nH_{2n}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:Alkenes: C n H 2 n|id=key-2>> We write that as the general formula C n H two n. So if you tell me there are three carbons, I instantly know there are six hydrogens. <<PAUSE:short>> Watch it work. Ethene has two carbons, so four hydrogens. Propene has three carbons, so six hydrogens. Each step adds one carbon and two hydrogens, the same building block every time. So remember the two big ideas: every alkene carries that <<FOCUS:double-bond>> reactive carbon-to-carbon double bond, and they all obey the formula C n H two n. <<UNFOCUS>> Know the carbons, and the hydrogens fall right out. <<PAUSE:short>>

The double bond literally <<FOCUS:ethene-double-bond+ethane-extra-hydrogens>> costs the molecule one pair of hydrogen atoms. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> For an alkene with any number of carbons, you always get exactly twice as many hydrogen atoms as carbon atoms. <<WRITE_EQUATION:C_nH_{2n}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:Every alkene fits C-n-H-2-n because the double bond costs one pair of hydrogens|id=key-1>> That is why every member of the family, two carbons, three carbons, ten carbons, always lands on twice as many hydrogens as carbons. <<TOPIC_START:topic:chemistry:organic_chemistry:17_7>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:organic_chemistry:17_7:alcohol_family_builder>> The same stuff that fuels some cars, dissolves the scent in your perfume, and sits in alcoholic drinks is one single molecule — and it belongs to a family you can spot by one tiny tag of just two atoms. <<SECTION:What makes an alcohol?|id=sec-1>> Look at <<FOCUS:oh-group>> this little group right here: an oxygen joined to a hydrogen. <<UNFOCUS>> We call it the O-H group, and it is the secret handshake of the entire family. <<PAUSE:short>> Whenever you see that O-H group <<FOCUS:oh-group+carbon-chain>> hanging off a carbon chain, you are looking at an alcohol — full stop. <<WRITE_TEXT:O-H group on a carbon chain = alcohol|id=text-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> Here is the smallest one possible: <<FOCUS:methanol-molecule>> a single carbon, wearing its hydrogens, with that O-H group on the end. <<UNFOCUS>> This is methanol. Now watch what happens when I <<FOCUS:added-carbon>> add just one more carbon to the chain. The O-H group <<FOCUS:oh-group>> stays exactly where it is — it never changes. What we have <<FOCUS:ethanol-molecule>> built now is ethanol, the alcohol in drinks and in that perfume solvent. <<UNFOCUS>> Notice nothing important changed except the chain got one carbon longer. So if every single member is just a chain of carbons with their hydrogens, capped by the same O-H group, could we write one formula that describes the whole family at once? <<PAUSE:long>> Because every member is just a <<FOCUS:carbon-chain>> chain of n carbons with their hydrogens, capped by the O-H group, we can write one formula that covers the whole family at once. <<WRITE_EQUATION:C_nH_{2n+1}OH|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:One pattern for the whole family|id=sec-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> We can. For n carbon atoms you get n carbons, two n plus one hydrogens, and the O-H. That is why we call them a homologous series — a family that follows a regular, predictable pattern. <<WRITE_KEY:General formula: C n H two n plus one O H|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> And because each step adds exactly one carbon and two hydrogens, the properties march along in step too. The boiling points climb steadily as the chains get longer — from sixty-five degrees Celsius, to seventy-eight, to eighty-seven, to one hundred seventeen. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter on making ethanol the biological way. We start with glucose, that's C six H twelve O six, in aqueous solution. Using yeast, the reaction is carried out in the absence of air, and it turns that glucose into ethanol. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How is ethanol made from glucose by fermentation?|id=ex-q-1>> Now, yeast is a mass of living cells, and the enzymes inside it catalyse the reaction. One molecule of glucose breaks down to produce two molecules of ethanol, that's C two H five O H, and two molecules of carbon dioxide, C O two. Let's write that equation down. <<WRITE_STEP:Glucose C6H12O6 (aq) -> 2 C2H5OH (aq) + 2 CO2 (g) + energy|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:C_6H_{12}O_6\,(aq) \rightarrow 2\,C_2H_5OH\,(aq) + 2\,CO_2\,(g) + \text{energy}|id=ex-eq-1>> Notice that the reaction also releases energy, so it is exothermic. This whole process is called fermentation. Finally, the ethanol is separated from the mixture by fractional distillation. So the answer: glucose ferments to give two molecules of ethanol plus two molecules of carbon dioxide plus energy, then the ethanol is recovered by fractional distillation. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Fermentation: C6H12O6 -> 2 C2H5OH + 2 CO2 + energy; ethanol separated by fractional distillation|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We want to make ethanol the chemical way, by the hydration of ethene. Hydration means water is added on, so this is an addition reaction where ethene, C two H four, reacts with water, H two O. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How is ethanol made by hydration of ethene?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by writing the reaction. Ethene gas plus water vapour gives ethanol, a liquid. This is carried out at a temperature of five hundred and seventy degrees Celsius and a pressure of sixty to seventy atmospheres, using a catalyst of phosphoric acid. <<WRITE_STEP:C2H4 (g) + H2O (g) -> C2H5OH (l)|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Conditions: 570 degrees C, 60-70 atm, phosphoric acid catalyst|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now notice the reaction is reversible and exothermic. In theory, high pressure and a low temperature would give the best yield. But in practice a high temperature of five hundred and seventy degrees Celsius is used to give a good rate of reaction, and the phosphoric acid catalyst speeds it up further. So the answer is: ethanol is made by adding water to ethene at five hundred and seventy degrees Celsius and sixty to seventy atmospheres over a phosphoric acid catalyst, in a reversible, exothermic addition reaction. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Ethanol made by hydration of ethene: C2H4 + H2O -> C2H5OH, at 570 C, 60-70 atm, phosphoric acid catalyst (reversible, exothermic)|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We take one molecule of liquid ethanol, C two H five O H, and burn it in oxygen. The question is: what does it produce, and why does that make it a good fuel? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Combustion of ethanol in oxygen|id=ex-q-1>> We start by writing the reactants. One molecule of ethanol reacts with three molecules of oxygen, O two. <<WRITE_STEP:C2H5OH (l) + 3 O2 (g) -> ...|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now we balance the products. The carbons go into carbon dioxide, giving two molecules of carbon dioxide, C O two, and the hydrogens go into water, giving three molecules of liquid water, H two O. Crucially, the reaction also releases heat. <<WRITE_STEP:... -> 2 CO2 (g) + 3 H2O (l) + heat|id=ex-step-1-2>> And so the answer is: one molecule of ethanol plus three molecules of oxygen gives two molecules of carbon dioxide, three molecules of water, and heat. Here is the simplest one of all, <<FOCUS:methanoic-chain>> methanoic acid, just a single carbon wearing that carboxyl group. Now watch what happens when we add one more carbon: <<FOCUS:ethanoic-chain>> we get ethanoic acid, the acid that makes vinegar sour, and notice <<FOCUS:carboxyl-group>> the carboxyl group on the end has not changed at all. <<WRITE_TEXT:chain grows, carboxyl group stays|id=text-2>> So here is the pattern of the whole family: <<FOCUS:carbon-chain>> only the carbon chain grows, one atom at a time, while <<FOCUS:carboxyl-group>> this same group stays bolted on the end. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> If only the chain length changes, could we capture every single member with one tidy formula? <<PAUSE:long>> Because every member is just a carboxyl group with a growing carbon chain, we can write one formula that fits them all: take any number of carbons n, give it twice as many hydrogens, and exactly two oxygens. <<WRITE_EQUATION:C_nH_{2n}O_2|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:General formula C n H two n O two|id=key-1>> Yes we can, and here it is: C n H two n O two, where n is just the number of carbons, two oxygens always, because that is the carboxyl group counted in. <<PAUSE:short>> A family like this, where each member differs from the next by one carbon and they all obey one general formula, is called a homologous series. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter. The carboxylic acids form a homologous series with the general formula C n H two n O two, and every member carries the same functional group, COOH, the carboxyl group. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Show how the boiling points of the carboxylic acids change as the molecules get bigger.|id=ex-q-1>> Let's line up the first four members by their number of carbon atoms and <<FOCUS:boiling-trend>> read off their boiling points. <<UNFOCUS>> Methanoic acid has one carbon atom and boils at one hundred and one degrees Celsius. Ethanoic acid has two carbon atoms and boils at one hundred and eighteen degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Methanoic acid, 1 carbon, boiling point 101 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Ethanoic acid, 2 carbons, boiling point 118 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now the next two. Propanoic acid has three carbon atoms and boils at one hundred and forty-one degrees Celsius, and butanoic acid has four carbon atoms and boils at one hundred and sixty-four degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Propanoic acid, 3 carbons, boiling point 141 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<WRITE_STEP:Butanoic acid, 4 carbons, boiling point 164 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-4>> So as the molecules get bigger, from one carbon up to four carbons, <<TRACE:boiling-trend>> the boiling point climbs steadily, from one hundred and one degrees Celsius all the way up to one hundred and sixty-four degrees Celsius. <<UNFOCUS>> The boiling points of the carboxylic acids rise as the molecules get bigger. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Boiling points rise with size: 101, 118, 141, 164 degrees Celsius for 1 to 4 carbons|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We oxidise ethanol much faster by warming it with a powerful oxidising agent, potassium manganate seven, in the presence of acid. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Oxidise ethanol to ethanoic acid using potassium manganate(VII) in acid — what is the colour change?|id=ex-q-1>> The manganate seven ions are themselves reduced to Mn two plus ions, and the acid provides the H plus ions for the reaction. <<WRITE_STEP:Acid provides H+ ions for the reaction|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:MnO_4^- + 8H^+ + 5e^- \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O|id=ex-eq-1>> So the colour change tells us it has worked: with potassium manganate seven the colour goes from purple to colourless. And potassium dichromate six could be used as an alternative oxidising agent, giving a colour change from orange to green. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Potassium manganate(VII): purple → colourless. Alternative — potassium dichromate(VI): orange → green.|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We're looking at a solution of ethanoic acid in water, and we want to understand why it behaves the way it does. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Why is ethanoic acid a weak acid?|id=ex-q-1>> When ethanoic acid is put in water, some of its molecules dissociate. Each molecule that dissociates splits into an ethanoate ion and a hydrogen ion. So ethanoic acid breaks apart into ethanoate ions plus hydrogen ions. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\mathrm{CH_3COOH\,(aq) \rightarrow CH_3COO^-\,(aq) + H^+\,(aq)}|id=ex-eq-1>> Now here's the key point. Only some of the molecules dissociate in this way, not all of them. Notice the reaction is reversible, and the sulfuric acid acts as a catalyst. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Propyl ethanoate (an ester, smells of pears) + water; reversible, sulfuric acid catalyst|id=ex-ans-1>> And because the molecules get heavier as the chain grows, look how <<TRACE:boiling-trend>> their boiling points climb steadily, from around one hundred one degrees Celsius for the smallest up to one hundred sixty four degrees for butanoic acid. So the next time vinegar makes your eyes water, remember it is <<FOCUS:carboxyl-group>> this one little carboxyl group doing the work, the same group hiding in every acid in the family. <<PAUSE:short>>

lecture_plan.chapter_arc: We begin with fossil fuels—where they come from and how crude oil is refined into useful products—then zoom in on the molecules themselves. From there the chapter builds the logic of organic chemistry: how millions of carbon compounds are organized into families, starting with the simple alkanes and moving through alkenes, alcohols, and carboxylic acids. The throughline is that one element, carbon, plus a system of families and functional groups, explains everything from the fuel in a car to the alcohol in a drink.
lecture_plan.opening_hook: The fuel in a car today started out as living plants and animals that died millions of years ago—so how does ancient life become petrol, and why is carbon the one element behind it all?

coverage_checklist.description: Explain how fossil fuels (petroleum, coal, natural gas) formed from ancient organisms over millions of years
Describe fractional distillation: crude oil as a mixture of hydrocarbons separated into fractions by boiling point
Cover post-distillation treatment—removing sulfur impurities and cracking long hydrocarbons into smaller useful molecules
Establish the organizing system of organic chemistry: families, functional groups, homologous series and general formulae
Distinguish saturated alkanes (single bonds) from unsaturated alkenes (C=C double bond) and link this to reactivity
Introduce the alcohol O-H functional group and the carboxylic acid family, identifying each by its functional group
Show how naming and general formulae let you predict any member of a family without memorizing each compound

lecture_plan.closing_summary: We started with a strange idea—that the petrol in a car was once living plants and animals—and we've followed carbon all the way from the oil well to the chemistry lab. You've seen how crude oil is separated by fractional distillation, treated and cracked into useful fuels, and then how chemists tame the millions of carbon compounds by sorting them into families. Each family—alkanes, alkenes, alcohols, carboxylic acids—is recognized by its functional group and follows a tidy homologous-series pattern, so once you know the rules you can name and predict compounds you've never seen. That's the power of organic chemistry: one element, a handful of families, and a logical system that connects ancient life to the molecules all around you.

segments.narration_chapter: The petrol burning in a car engine today was once living creatures, swimming in an ocean millions of years ago, long before the dinosaurs. <<SECTION:Fossil fuels|id=sec-1>> When those tiny organisms died, they sank to the sea floor and got buried under thick layers of sediment, deeper and deeper, year after year. Then, over millions of years, enormous pressure and heat slowly squeezed and cooked those buried remains into something new entirely. <<PAUSE:short>> That something is petroleum, also called crude oil — and along with coal and natural gas, it is what we call a fossil fuel, because it really is made from ancient fossils. <<PAUSE:short>> But here is the strange part: if you could smell a drop of crude oil, you would be smelling not one substance, but hundreds of different compounds all mixed together. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:organic_chemistry:17_1:hydrocarbon_skeletons>> <<SECTION:Hydrocarbons|id=sec-2>> So what are all these compounds made of? Almost all of them are built from just two kinds of atom — carbon and hydrogen — and <<FOCUS:carbon-chain>> we call those molecules hydrocarbons. <<PAUSE:short>> Watch this chain take shape. <<FOCUS:carbon-atom-label>> Each grey atom here is carbon, the backbone of the whole molecule. <<WRITE_TEXT:C = carbon, H = hydrogen|id=text-1>> This carbon, marked C, links to its neighbours, and every spare arm <<FOCUS:hydrogen-atom-label>> grabs a hydrogen atom, marked H. <<UNFOCUS>> Carbon and hydrogen — that is the whole recipe. <<PAUSE:short>> Now, why hundreds of different compounds? Because carbon is a master builder — the same atoms can connect <<FOCUS:carbon-chain>> in a straight chain, or <<FOCUS:carbon-ring>> curl right around into a ring. <<UNFOCUS>> Short chains, long chains, rings, branches — each different shape is a different compound, which is exactly why crude oil is such a rich mixture. <<WRITE_KEY:Petroleum = a mixture of hydrocarbons (carbon + hydrogen)|id=key-1>> So remember this: petroleum is not one chemical, it is a mixture of hydrocarbons, molecules made only from carbon and hydrogen. <<PAUSE:short>> And every time you fill a tank, you are burning carbon chains that took an ocean, a graveyard of ancient life, and millions of years of pressure to build.

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:organic_chemistry:17_2:distillation_column>> Pump crude oil out of the ground and you don't get fuel — you get a <<FOCUS:crude-oil-flask>> thick black soup of hundreds of different molecules, all jumbled together. Every one of those molecules is a hydrocarbon — built only from hydrogen and carbon — but they come in wildly different sizes, <<FOCUS:small-molecule+large-molecule>> from tiny short chains to enormous long ones. <<WRITE_TEXT:Crude oil = mixture of many hydrocarbons|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> A giant jumbled mixture like this is almost useless, so our first job is to sort it — and the trick is hiding in how these molecules behave when you heat them. Here's the question: if I <<FOCUS:heat-source>> gently warm this whole mixture, which molecules do you think escape the liquid first? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The small, light ones. They're loosely held, so it takes only a little energy to free them — <<FOCUS:small-molecule>> they boil off first, at low temperatures. The <<FOCUS:large-molecule>> big heavy molecules cling on and need far more heat to escape. <<WRITE_KEY:Small molecules boil first (low temp); big molecules need high temp|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> So we heat the crude oil and <<TRACE:rising-vapour>> let the vapours rise up through a tall column that's <<FOCUS:temp-bot-label+temp-top-label>> hot at the bottom and cool at the top. <<UNFOCUS>> As a vapour climbs and cools, it condenses back into a liquid the moment it reaches its own boiling temperature — and we collect it there. <<WRITE_TEXT:Vapour condenses where it cools to its boiling point|id=text-2>> The lightest molecules stay as gas highest up and are <<FOCUS:fraction-light>> caught at the cool top of the column. The heaviest molecules barely rise at all — they condense low down where it's still scorching hot, and are <<FOCUS:fraction-heavy>> drawn off at the bottom. <<SECTION:The fractions|id=sec-2>> Because the lighter molecules boil at lower temperatures, <<FOCUS:column>> each height in the column traps molecules of one particular size — that's exactly why the sorting works. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter: refining petroleum in the lab. We gently heat the petroleum and let the compounds evaporate, collecting what condenses in cool test-tubes. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Refine petroleum by collecting fractions as the thermometer rises|id=ex-q-1>> We start by watching what evaporates first. The smaller, lighter molecules go first, since it takes less energy to free them from the liquid. As the hot vapours rise, so does the thermometer reading. When the reading reaches one hundred degrees Celsius, we swap the first test-tube for an empty one, and that liquid is our first fraction. <<WRITE_STEP:Smaller lighter molecules evaporate first - swap first test-tube at 100 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-1>> Then we collect three more fractions in the same way, swapping the test-tube at one hundred and fifty degrees Celsius, at two hundred degrees Celsius, and at three hundred degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Swap again at 150, 200, and 300 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-2>> And the answer is that we end up with four fractions collected in total, each gathered over a rising temperature range. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Four fractions collected total, at 100, 150, 200, and 300 degrees Celsius|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We're comparing four fractions collected from distillation, and we want to see how their properties change as the molecules get larger. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How do the four fractions compare in boiling point, runniness, volatility, and flammability?|id=ex-q-1>> Let's lay them out in order. Fraction one boils up to one hundred degrees Celsius, it's very runny, very volatile, burns very easily, and it's made of small molecules. <<WRITE_STEP:Fraction 1: bp up to 100 C, very runny, volatile, burns very easily, small molecules|id=ex-step-1-1>> Fraction two boils between one hundred and one hundred fifty degrees Celsius, it's runny, less volatile, and burns easily. <<WRITE_STEP:Fraction 2: bp 100 to 150 C, runny, less volatile, burns easily|id=ex-step-1-2>> Continuing down, fraction three boils between one hundred fifty and two hundred degrees Celsius, it's not very runny, even less volatile, and it does not burn easily. <<WRITE_STEP:Fraction 3: bp 150 to 200 C, not very runny, even less volatile, not easily burns|id=ex-step-1-3>> And fraction four boils between two hundred and three hundred degrees Celsius, it's viscous, thick and sticky, the least volatile, it only burns with a wick, and it's made of large molecules. <<WRITE_STEP:Fraction 4: bp 200 to 300 C, viscous, least volatile, burns only with a wick, large molecules|id=ex-step-1-4>> So the pattern is clear: as the molecules get larger from fraction one through fraction four, the boiling point rises while runniness, volatility, and flammability all decrease together. <<WRITE_ANSWER:As molecules get larger (Fraction 1 to 4), boiling point rises; runniness, volatility, and flammability all decrease.|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. A fractional distillation tower separates crude oil by the size of the molecules. At the base it's over four hundred degrees Celsius, and near the top it's about twenty-five degrees Celsius. The bigger molecules condense low down where it's hot, and the smaller ones rise to the cooler top. Let's list the fractions from lightest to heaviest. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Name each refinery fraction by its carbon range and its use.|id=ex-q-1>> We start at the top of the tower with the smallest molecules. Refinery gas has one to four carbon atoms and is used as bottled gas for cooking and heating. <<WRITE_STEP:Refinery gas: C1 to C4, cooking and heating gas|id=ex-step-1-1>> Next is gasoline, or petrol, with five to six carbon atoms, used as fuel for cars. <<WRITE_STEP:Gasoline (petrol): C5 to C6, car fuel|id=ex-step-1-2>> Then naphtha, six to ten carbon atoms, the feedstock for many chemicals and plastics. <<WRITE_STEP:Naphtha: C6 to C10, chemicals and plastics feedstock|id=ex-step-1-3>> Moving down where it's warmer, paraffin, also called kerosene, has ten to fifteen carbon atoms and fuels aircraft and lamps. <<WRITE_STEP:Paraffin (kerosene): C10 to C15, aircraft and lamp fuel|id=ex-step-1-4>> Diesel oil has fifteen to twenty carbon atoms for diesel engines. <<WRITE_STEP:Diesel oil: C15 to C20, diesel engine fuel|id=ex-step-1-5>> Fuel oil has twenty to thirty carbon atoms for power stations and ships. <<WRITE_STEP:Fuel oil: C20 to C30, power stations and ships|id=ex-step-1-6>> Finally, at the hot base of the tower, the heaviest molecules. The lubricating fraction has thirty to fifty carbon atoms, giving engine oil and waxes. <<WRITE_STEP:Lubricating fraction: C30 to C50, engine oil and waxes|id=ex-step-1-7>> And bitumen, with fifty carbon atoms upwards, is used for road surfaces and roofs. <<WRITE_STEP:Bitumen: C50 upwards, road surfaces and roofs|id=ex-step-1-8>> So the full set of fractions, from refinery gas at one to four carbon atoms up top, down to bitumen at fifty carbons and beyond at the base. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Eight fractions: refinery gas (C1-C4) to bitumen (C50+), heaviest at the hot base, lightest at the cool top|id=ex-ans-1>> This whole process of separating crude oil into groups of similar-sized molecules has a name: fractional distillation, and the groups we collect are called fractions. <<WRITE_KEY:Fractional distillation sorts crude oil into fractions by boiling point|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> And that's the magic: one black useless soup goes in, and out come neat fractions — from runny, easily-burning fuels at the top to thick, heavy oils at the bottom — each one sorted purely by how easily its molecules let go of the liquid. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:organic_chemistry:17_3:cracking_split>> Crude oil gives us far too much thick, heavy gloop that nobody wants, and never enough of the light petrol everyone is desperate for. So how do we turn the useless into the valuable? <<SECTION:Cracking|id=sec-1>> Here is the heavy stuff: <<FOCUS:long-chain>> a hydrocarbon with a long chain of carbon atoms. <<UNFOCUS>> Long chains mean a high boiling point, hard to set alight, not much use as a fuel. <<PAUSE:short>> Now imagine heating it really hard, and passing it over a hot catalyst. Something has to give. Where do you think <<FOCUS:break-point>> this long chain will break? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Cracking = breaking large hydrocarbons into smaller, more useful ones|id=key-1>> It snaps in the middle. The chain breaks <<FOCUS:small-alkane+small-alkene>> into two smaller pieces, and that is cracking: breaking big molecules into smaller, more useful ones. <<PAUSE:short>> On this side we get <<FOCUS:small-alkane>> a short chain where every carbon already holds all the hydrogen it can. <<UNFOCUS>> We call that an alkane, and it is exactly the smaller, lighter fuel we wanted. But here is the catch. When the chain snapped, <<FOCUS:small-alkene>> this other piece was left short of hydrogen. <<UNFOCUS>> Two of its carbons grab each other extra tightly instead. <<WRITE_TEXT:alkene = has a C=C double bond|id=text-1>> That extra-tight grip is <<FOCUS:double-bond>> a double bond between two carbon atoms. <<UNFOCUS>> A molecule with a carbon-to-carbon double bond is called an alkene. segments.narration_chapter: There are more than ten million known organic compounds — and yet you will never have to memorize a single one of their names, because every name is secretly a code. Here is the trick that chemists worked out: instead of inventing a random name for each compound, they built the name out of two clues stuck together. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:organic_chemistry:17_4:name_decoder>> <<SECTION:The hidden code|id=sec-1>> Look at this name on the board — <<FOCUS:full-name>> propanol. It looks like one word, but it is <<FOCUS:split-line>> really two pieces of information glued together. The ending of the name — <<FOCUS:suffix-part>> the very last part — tells you which family the compound belongs to. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> If a name ends in -ane it is an alkane, if it ends in -ene it is an alkene, if it ends in -ol it is an alcohol, and if it ends in -oic acid it is a carboxylic acid. <<PAUSE:short>> So <<FOCUS:suffix-part>> this ending, -ol, immediately tells me: this compound is a member of <<FOCUS:family-tag>> the alcohol family. <<UNFOCUS>> I did not have to look anything up. Now, the family alone is not enough — alcohols come in many sizes. So what tells me how big this particular molecule is? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:prefix-part>> The beginning of the name carries that second clue. <<WRITE_TEXT:prefix = carbon count|id=text-1>> The prefix tells you exactly <<FOCUS:carbon-chain>> how many carbon atoms are in the chain. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Meth- means one carbon, eth- means two, prop- means three, and but- means four. So prop- tells me this molecule has exactly <<FOCUS:carbon-count-label>> three carbon atoms. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Name = (how many carbons) + (which family)|id=key-1>> Put the two clues together and the name decodes itself: <<FOCUS:prefix-part+suffix-part>> prop plus ol means a three-carbon molecule in the alcohol family. <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. For the alkanes, the general formula is C n H two n plus two, where n is just a number that tells you how many carbon atoms are in the molecule. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Use the general formula CnH2n+2 to find the formulas of methane, ethane, and propane|id=ex-q-1>> Let's start with methane. For methane, n is one. So we put one in for n, and two times one plus two gives four hydrogens. That's C one H four, which we write as CH four. <<WRITE_STEP:Methane: n = 1, so C1H(2x1+2) = CH4|id=ex-step-1-1>> Next, ethane. For ethane, n is two. Two carbons, and two times two plus two gives six hydrogens. So that's C two H six. <<WRITE_STEP:Ethane: n = 2, so C2H(2x2+2) = C2H6|id=ex-step-1-2>> And finally propane. For propane, n is three. Three carbons, and two times three plus two gives eight hydrogens. So that's C three H eight. <<WRITE_STEP:Propane: n = 3, so C3H(2x3+2) = C3H8|id=ex-step-1-3>> And there are our answers: methane is CH four, ethane is C two H six, and propane is C three H eight, all built straight from the general formula C n H two n plus two. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Methane CH4, Ethane C2H6, Propane C3H8|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Let's look at the first four members of the alkane family and watch what happens to their boiling points. Methane has one carbon atom, ethane has two carbon atoms, propane has three carbon atoms, and butane has four carbon atoms. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How does boiling point change from methane to butane?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by listing each one with its boiling point. Methane, with just one carbon, has the lowest boiling point at about minus one hundred sixty-four degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Methane (1 C): about -164 degrees C|id=ex-step-1-1>> Ethane, with two carbons, boils a little higher. <<WRITE_STEP:Ethane (2 C): higher than methane|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now we keep going up the chain. Propane, with three carbons, boils at about minus forty-two degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Propane (3 C): about -42 degrees C|id=ex-step-1-3>> And butane, with four carbons, boils at about minus zero point five degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Butane (4 C): about -0.5 degrees C|id=ex-step-1-4>> Look at the pattern: each time we add a carbon, the boiling point climbs. So the answer is clear, the boiling point increases as the chain length increases. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Boiling point increases as chain length increases (methane < ethane < propane < butane)|id=ex-ans-1>> And the simplest family of all, the alkanes, shows the pattern beautifully: methane has one carbon, ethane two, propane three, butane four — and as the chains get longer, the boiling points climb steadily upward. So once you know the endings and the beginnings, you have not learned one compound — you have learned how to read millions of them at a glance.

segments.narration_chapter: The gas that cooks your dinner, the fuel in a camping stove, the stuff inside a cigarette lighter, they all come from one single family of molecules built from just two ingredients. <<SECTION:The Alkanes|id=sec-1>> Those two ingredients are carbon and hydrogen, and a molecule made of only carbon and hydrogen has a special name, a hydrocarbon. <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:organic_chemistry:17_5:ethane_bonding>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Hydrocarbon = carbon + hydrogen only|id=text-1>> The alkanes are the simplest hydrocarbons of all, and the cleanest way to meet them is to look at one molecule up close. Here is ethane, and you can see its skeleton is just <<FOCUS:carbon-left+carbon-right>> two carbon atoms, with <<FOCUS:hydrogens>> hydrogen atoms hanging off the outside, nothing else in the whole molecule. Now look right at the middle, at <<FOCUS:cc-bond>> the link joining the two carbons together. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> That link is one shared pair of electrons, and one shared pair is exactly what we mean by a single bond. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Every C-C bond is single, so alkanes are saturated|id=key-1>> And this is the rule for the whole family: every carbon-to-carbon bond is a single bond, with no spare bonds left over, which is why we call the alkanes saturated. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:A family with a pattern|id=sec-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> The alkanes aren't just one molecule though, they're a whole series, and the series follows a beautifully simple pattern. Start with methane, one carbon. Add a carbon and two hydrogens and you get ethane. Add another carbon and two more hydrogens and you get propane. So if I just told you a molecule has ten carbons, could you tell me exactly how many hydrogens it must have, without ever seeing it? <<PAUSE:long>> Because each member differs from the next by one carbon and two hydrogens, the number of hydrogens is always two times the number of carbons, plus two more. <<WRITE_EQUATION:C_nH_{2n+2}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Each step: +1 carbon, +2 hydrogens|id=key-2>> Yes, you can, because each member differs from the next by one carbon and two hydrogens, and that locks in the formula carbon-n hydrogen two-n-plus-two. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter. When methane burns in a good supply of oxygen, it undergoes complete combustion. We start with one molecule of methane, that's C H four, reacting with two molecules of oxygen, two O two. The reaction needs that good supply of oxygen to burn cleanly. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What is the complete combustion of methane?|id=ex-q-1>> Now we write the reactants on the left. One methane molecule plus two oxygen molecules. <<WRITE_STEP:Reactants: one C H four plus two O two|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow|id=ex-eq-1>> These react together to form the products. One molecule of methane gives one carbon dioxide, that's one C O two, plus two molecules of water, two H two O, and it releases plenty of heat energy. So the answer is: C H four plus two O two gives one C O two plus two H two O plus heat energy. <<WRITE_ANSWER:CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O + heat energy|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. When there isn't enough oxygen, alkanes undergo incomplete combustion, and instead of carbon dioxide they produce poisonous carbon monoxide. Let's balance the equation for methane burning in too little oxygen. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Write the incomplete combustion of methane in insufficient oxygen|id=ex-q-1>> We start on the left side with two molecules of methane reacting with three molecules of oxygen. Because there isn't enough oxygen, the carbon can't fully oxidise. <<WRITE_STEP:2 CH4 + 3 O2 -> ?|id=ex-step-1-1>> Working out the products: the carbon ends up as carbon monoxide, so we get two molecules of carbon monoxide, and the hydrogen forms four molecules of water. And critically, this reaction releases less heat energy than complete combustion, all because there is not enough oxygen. <<WRITE_STEP:Products: 2 CO + 4 H2O + less heat|id=ex-step-1-2>> And the answer is the balanced equation: two methane plus three oxygen gives two carbon monoxide plus four water, releasing less heat energy. <<WRITE_ANSWER:2 CH4 (g) + 3 O2 (g) -> 2 CO (g) + 4 H2O (l) + less heat energy|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Methane reacts with chlorine, that's C-l-two, but only in sunlight. The light is essential because it breaks the chlorine bonds, so this is a photochemical reaction. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What happens when methane reacts with chlorine in sunlight?|id=ex-q-1>> We start with the first reaction. In sunlight, methane plus chlorine produces chloromethane, C-H-three-C-l, plus hydrogen chloride, H-C-l. We call this a substitution reaction, because a chlorine atom takes the place of a hydrogen atom. <<WRITE_STEP:methane + Cl2 --(light)--> chloromethane (CH3Cl) + HCl|id=ex-step-1-1>> And if there's enough chlorine, all four hydrogen atoms get replaced, one by one, giving a whole series: chloromethane C-H-three-C-l, then dichloromethane C-H-two-C-l-two, then trichloromethane C-H-C-l-three, and finally tetrachloromethane C-C-l-four. <<WRITE_ANSWER:CH3Cl, then CH2Cl2, then CHCl3, then CCl4|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Take two alkanes that share the exact same formula, C four H ten. The first is butane, which has a straight, unbranched chain. The second is two-methylpropane, where the chain is branched. They're isomers — same formula, different structure. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Butane and 2-methylpropane both have formula C4H10. Compare their boiling points.|id=ex-q-1>> Let's compare their boiling points. Butane, the straight-chain molecule, boils at zero degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Butane (straight chain): boiling point = 0 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-1>> The branched one, two-methylpropane, boils at minus ten degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:2-methylpropane (branched): boiling point = -10 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-2>> So the branched isomer has the lower boiling point. <<WRITE_STEP:Branched isomer has the lower boiling point|id=ex-step-1-3>> Why? Because branching reduces the attraction between molecules — the branches make it harder for the molecules to get close to each other, so less energy is needed to pull them apart. That's the takeaway: the branched isomer, two-methylpropane, boils lower at minus ten degrees Celsius, because branching reduces attraction between molecules. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Branched 2-methylpropane boils lower (-10 degrees Celsius vs 0 degrees Celsius for butane), because branching reduces attraction between molecules.|id=ex-ans-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Ten carbons: 2 times 10 plus 2 = 22 hydrogens|id=step-1>> For ten carbons, two times ten plus two gives twenty-two hydrogens, so the molecule is carbon ten hydrogen twenty-two, and you never had to draw it. <<PAUSE:short>> So a family built from only carbon and hydrogen, joined entirely by single bonds, marching up in steps of one carbon and two hydrogens, that, in one breath, is what an alkane is. <<PAUSE:short>>

Here is ethane, and you can see its skeleton is just two carbon atoms, with hydrogen atoms hanging off the outside, nothing else in the whole molecule. <<POINT:hydrogens>> <<POINT:hydrogens>> <<FOCUS:cc-bond>> Now look right at the middle, at the link joining the two carbons together. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> That link is one shared pair of electrons, and one shared pair is exactly what we mean by a single bond. <<TRACE:cc-bond>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:cc-bond>> <<WRITE_KEY:Every C-C bond is single, so alkanes are saturated|id=key-1>>And this is the rule for the whole family: every carbon-to-carbon bond is a single bond, with no spare bonds left over, which is why we call the alkanes saturated. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:A family with a pattern|id=sec-2>>The alkanes aren't just one molecule though, they're a whole series, and the series follows a beautifully simple pattern. Start with methane, one carbon. Add a carbon and two hydrogens and you get ethane. Add another carbon and two more hydrogens and you get propane. So if I just told you a molecule has ten carbons, could you tell me exactly how many hydrogens it must have, without ever seeing it? <<PAUSE:long>> Because each member differs from the next by one carbon and two hydrogens, the number of hydrogens is always two times the number of carbons, plus two more. <<WRITE_EQUATION:C_nH_{2n+2}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Each step: +1 carbon, +2 hydrogens|id=key-2>>Yes, you can, because each member differs from the next by one carbon and two hydrogens, and that locks in the formula carbon-n hydrogen two-n-plus-two. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter. When methane burns in a good supply of oxygen, it undergoes complete combustion. We start with one molecule of methane, that's C H four, reacting with two molecules of oxygen, two O two. The reaction needs that good supply of oxygen to burn cleanly. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What is the complete combustion of methane?|id=ex-q-1>> Now we write the reactants on the left. One methane molecule plus two oxygen molecules. <<WRITE_STEP:Reactants: one C H four plus two O two|id=ex-step-1-1>><<WRITE_EQUATION:CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow|id=ex-eq-1>> These react together to form the products. segments.narration_chapter: What if one tiny change in how two carbon atoms hold hands could turn an ordinary, sleepy chemical into a far more reactive one? <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:organic_chemistry:17_6:ethene_bonding>> Meet the alkenes, a family of compounds built from only two elements, carbon and hydrogen. <<SECTION:The alkene family|id=sec-1>> Because they contain only those two elements, we call them hydrocarbons. Here is the simplest alkene, <<FOCUS:carbon-left+carbon-right>> called ethene. Two carbon atoms sitting in the middle, with <<FOCUS:hydrogen-atoms>> hydrogen atoms hanging off the sides. Now look right here, <<FOCUS:double-bond>> between the two carbons. <<UNFOCUS>> There are not one but two lines joining them. That is a carbon-to-carbon double bond, <<FOCUS:double-bond-label>> two shared pairs of electrons instead of one. <<WRITE_KEY:Every alkene has a C=C double bond, its functional group|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> This double bond is the single most important feature of the whole family.
