segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:organic_chemistry:26_5:ethene_vs_ethane>> Here are two molecules. One sits in a jar for years doing nothing; the other grabs onto almost anything you throw at it. Same two ingredients, carbon and hydrogen, so what makes the difference? <<PAUSE:long>> Look <<FOCUS:ethene-double-bond>> right at the centre of this molecule. The two carbon atoms are joined not by one line, but by two. <<UNFOCUS>> That is a double bond, and it is the entire story of the alkenes. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Counting the hydrogens|id=sec-1>> Now let us count. This molecule <<FOCUS:ethene-carbon-left+ethene-carbon-right>> is ethene. Each carbon holds <<FOCUS:ethene-hydrogens>> two hydrogen atoms, so four hydrogens in total around two carbons. Beside it <<FOCUS:ethane-single-bond>> is ethane, the lazy one. Its carbons are joined by a single bond, and look, it has room for <<FOCUS:ethane-extra-hydrogens>> two extra hydrogen atoms that ethene simply does not have. <<UNFOCUS>> So why does an alkene always have exactly twice as many hydrogens as carbons, the pattern we write as C-n-H-2-n? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Because making <<FOCUS:ethene-double-bond>> that second bond between the carbons uses up a pair of hands that would otherwise hold hydrogens. The double bond literally <<FOCUS:ethene-double-bond+ethane-extra-hydrogens>> costs the molecule one pair of hydrogen atoms. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> For an alkene with any number of carbons, you always get exactly twice as many hydrogen atoms as carbon atoms. <<WRITE_EQUATION:C_nH_{2n}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:Every alkene fits C-n-H-2-n because the double bond costs one pair of hydrogens|id=key-1>> That is why every member of the family, two carbons, three carbons, ten carbons, always lands on twice as many hydrogens as carbons. The formula is C-n-H-2-n, and now you can see exactly where it comes from. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Why alkenes are so reactive|id=sec-2>> Now here is the beautiful part. Picture that double bond as a doorway. One of the two bonds <<FOCUS:ethene-double-bond>> can swing open, leaving each carbon with a free hand ready to grab a new atom. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:double bond opens, atoms add on|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> When that doorway opens and new atoms attach, we call it an addition reaction. Ethene can add hydrogen back on to become ethane, or add water to become ethanol. Here's an example from the chapter. We make alkenes from alkanes by a process called cracking. In this case, our starting material is ethane, and we pass it together with steam over a catalyst at a temperature of over eight hundred degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Crack ethane with steam at over 800 C — what forms?|id=ex-q-1>> When we crack ethane under these conditions, the molecule breaks apart. The carbon chain rearranges to form a carbon-to-carbon double bond, giving us ethene, and at the same time a molecule of hydrogen is released. <<WRITE_STEP:ethane + steam, over 800 C → cracking|id=ex-step-1-1>> So the products are ethene and hydrogen. Ethane, with steam at over eight hundred degrees Celsius, gives ethene plus hydrogen. <<WRITE_ANSWER:ethane → ethene + hydrogen|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Ethene, which is a gas, reacts with hydrogen gas in an addition reaction. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What does ethene form when it reacts with hydrogen?|id=ex-q-1>> For this reaction to happen, we need a catalyst, along with heat and pressure. Under those conditions, the hydrogen adds across the double bond of ethene. <<WRITE_STEP:Ethene (gas) + hydrogen gas, with a catalyst, heat and pressure|id=ex-step-1-1>> The product is ethane gas, a saturated molecule. So the answer is: ethene plus hydrogen gives ethane gas. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Ethene + H2 -> ethane (gas)|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Ethene, which is a gas, reacts with water in the form of steam. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What does ethene form when it adds water across its double bond?|id=ex-q-1>> For this reaction to happen, we need a catalyst, along with heat and pressure. Under those conditions, ethene adds water across its double bond. <<WRITE_STEP:Ethene (gas) plus water as steam, with a catalyst, heat and pressure|id=ex-step-1>> And the product is ethanol, a liquid alcohol. <<WRITE_ANSWER:The product is ethanol, a liquid alcohol|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Take ethene as our starting molecule, the monomer, and let it undergo polymerisation. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Many ethene monomers join by polymerisation — what forms?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by joining many ethene molecules together. Each ethene monomer links to the next, opening its double bond so the units chain end to end. <<WRITE_STEP:Step 1: Many ethene monomers (the monomer) join by polymerisation.|id=ex-step-1-1>> And the answer is that the product is poly of ethene, also called polythene, and this chain can be many thousands of carbon atoms long. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Product = poly(ethene) / polythene — chains many thousands of carbon atoms long.|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Bromine water is an orange solution, and we use it to test whether a hydrocarbon is unsaturated. Take ethene, which is a gas, and bubble it through this orange bromine water. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What happens when ethene gas is bubbled through orange bromine water?|id=ex-q-1>> Ethene has a carbon-carbon double bond, so it reacts with bromine water in an addition reaction. The bromine adds straight across that double bond. <<WRITE_STEP:ethene (gas) + bromine water (orange) gives an addition reaction|id=ex-step-1-1>> The product is one-two-dibromoethane, which is colourless, so the orange colour disappears. <<WRITE_ANSWER:ethene + bromine water gives 1,2-dibromoethane (colourless) — the orange colour disappears|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We're asked to compare three compounds that all share the very same molecular formula, C four H eight. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Three compounds all have formula C4H8 but different structures. What are they?|id=ex-q-1>> So all three have formula C four H eight, but when we draw them out we find they have different structures and the double bond sits in different positions. That tells us straight away these are isomers of one another. <<WRITE_STEP:Same formula C4H8, different structures and double-bond positions -> isomers|id=ex-step-1>> And the answer is that the three isomers are but-one-ene, but-two-ene, and two-methylpropene, all members of the alkene family. <<WRITE_ANSWER:The three C4H8 isomers are but-1-ene, but-2-ene and 2-methylpropene|id=ex-ans-1>> A molecule with a double bond waiting to open is called unsaturated. Once it has grabbed its extra atoms and the doorway is shut, it is saturated, just like the lazy alkane next door. <<PAUSE:short>> So that is the whole secret. The double bond costs an alkene one pair of hydrogens, giving the formula C-n-H-2-n, and that same double bond is the open doorway that makes alkenes far more reactive than alkanes.

segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:organic_chemistry:17_7:alcohol_family_builder>> The same stuff that fuels some cars, dissolves the scent in your perfume, and sits in alcoholic drinks is one single molecule — and it belongs to a family you can spot by one tiny tag of just two atoms. <<SECTION:What makes an alcohol?|id=sec-1>> Look at <<FOCUS:oh-group>> this little group right here: an oxygen joined to a hydrogen. <<UNFOCUS>> We call it the O-H group, and it is the secret handshake of the entire family. <<PAUSE:short>> Whenever you see that O-H group <<FOCUS:oh-group+carbon-chain>> hanging off a carbon chain, you are looking at an alcohol — full stop. <<WRITE_TEXT:O-H group on a carbon chain = alcohol|id=text-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> Here is the smallest one possible: <<FOCUS:methanol-molecule>> a single carbon, wearing its hydrogens, with that O-H group on the end. <<UNFOCUS>> This is methanol. Now watch what happens when I <<FOCUS:added-carbon>> add just one more carbon to the chain. The O-H group <<FOCUS:oh-group>> stays exactly where it is — it never changes. What we have <<FOCUS:ethanol-molecule>> built now is ethanol, the alcohol in drinks and in that perfume solvent. <<UNFOCUS>> Notice nothing important changed except the chain got one carbon longer. segments.narration_chapter: <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:organic_chemistry:17_8:carboxyl_family>> That sour sting in your vinegar, the tang in sour milk, the bite of a stinging nettle, they all come from the same little cluster of atoms. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:The carboxyl group|id=sec-1>> This cluster is a carbon joined to two oxygens in a special way, one by a double bond and one carrying a hydrogen, and <<FOCUS:carboxyl-group>> we write it as C-O-O-H. <<WRITE_TEXT:C-O-O-H = the carboxyl group|id=text-1>> Wherever you find this group, you have a carboxylic acid, an organic acid, and we call this group the carboxyl group. Here is the simplest one of all, <<FOCUS:methanoic-chain>> methanoic acid, just a single carbon wearing that carboxyl group. Now watch what happens when we add one more carbon: <<FOCUS:ethanoic-chain>> we get ethanoic acid, the acid that makes vinegar sour, and notice <<FOCUS:carboxyl-group>> the carboxyl group on the end has not changed at all. <<WRITE_TEXT:chain grows, carboxyl group stays|id=text-2>> So here is the pattern of the whole family: <<FOCUS:carbon-chain>> only the carbon chain grows, one atom at a time, while <<FOCUS:carboxyl-group>> this same group stays bolted on the end. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> If only the chain length changes, could we capture every single member with one tidy formula? <<PAUSE:long>> Because every member is just a carboxyl group with a growing carbon chain, we can write one formula that fits them all: take any number of carbons n, give it twice as many hydrogens, and exactly two oxygens. <<WRITE_EQUATION:C_nH_{2n}O_2|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:General formula C n H two n O two|id=key-1>> Yes we can, and here it is: C n H two n O two, where n is just the number of carbons, two oxygens always, because that is the carboxyl group counted in. <<PAUSE:short>> A family like this, where each member differs from the next by one carbon and they all obey one general formula, is called a homologous series. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter. The carboxylic acids form a homologous series with the general formula C n H two n O two, and every member carries the same functional group, COOH, the carboxyl group. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Show how the boiling points of the carboxylic acids change as the molecules get bigger.|id=ex-q-1>> Let's line up the first four members by their number of carbon atoms and <<FOCUS:boiling-trend>> read off their boiling points. <<UNFOCUS>> Methanoic acid has one carbon atom and boils at one hundred and one degrees Celsius. Ethanoic acid has two carbon atoms and boils at one hundred and eighteen degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Methanoic acid, 1 carbon, boiling point 101 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Ethanoic acid, 2 carbons, boiling point 118 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now the next two. Propanoic acid has three carbon atoms and boils at one hundred and forty-one degrees Celsius, and butanoic acid has four carbon atoms and boils at one hundred and sixty-four degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Propanoic acid, 3 carbons, boiling point 141 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<WRITE_STEP:Butanoic acid, 4 carbons, boiling point 164 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-4>> So as the molecules get bigger, from one carbon up to four carbons, <<TRACE:boiling-trend>> the boiling point climbs steadily, from one hundred and one degrees Celsius all the way up to one hundred and sixty-four degrees Celsius. <<UNFOCUS>> The boiling points of the carboxylic acids rise as the molecules get bigger. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Boiling points rise with size: 101, 118, 141, 164 degrees Celsius for 1 to 4 carbons|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We oxidise ethanol much faster by warming it with a powerful oxidising agent, potassium manganate seven, in the presence of acid. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Oxidise ethanol to ethanoic acid using potassium manganate(VII) in acid — what is the colour change?|id=ex-q-1>> The manganate seven ions are themselves reduced to Mn two plus ions, and the acid provides the H plus ions for the reaction. <<WRITE_STEP:Acid provides H+ ions for the reaction|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:MnO_4^- + 8H^+ + 5e^- \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O|id=ex-eq-1>> So the colour change tells us it has worked: with potassium manganate seven the colour goes from purple to colourless. And potassium dichromate six could be used as an alternative oxidising agent, giving a colour change from orange to green. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Potassium manganate(VII): purple → colourless. Alternative — potassium dichromate(VI): orange → green.|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We're looking at a solution of ethanoic acid in water, and we want to understand why it behaves the way it does. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Why is ethanoic acid a weak acid?|id=ex-q-1>> When ethanoic acid is put in water, some of its molecules dissociate. Each molecule that dissociates splits into an ethanoate ion and a hydrogen ion. So ethanoic acid breaks apart into ethanoate ions plus hydrogen ions. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\mathrm{CH_3COOH\,(aq) \rightarrow CH_3COO^-\,(aq) + H^+\,(aq)}|id=ex-eq-1>> Now here's the key point. Only some of the molecules dissociate in this way, not all of them. Because only some molecules dissociate, ethanoic acid is a weak acid. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Ethanoic acid is a weak acid because only some of its molecules dissociate into ethanoate ions and hydrogen ions.|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Ethanoic acid reacts with sodium hydroxide, and we want to see why this shows ethanoic acid is a typical acid. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What happens when ethanoic acid reacts with sodium hydroxide?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by recognising the pattern. Sodium hydroxide is a base, and acids react with bases to form a salt plus water. So ethanoic acid plus sodium hydroxide gives sodium ethanoate plus water. <<WRITE_STEP:ethanoic acid + sodium hydroxide -> sodium ethanoate + water|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:CH_3COOH\,(aq) + NaOH\,(aq) \rightarrow CH_3COONa\,(aq) + H_2O\,(l)|id=ex-eq-1>> And the answer is that the products are sodium ethanoate and water. Sodium ethanoate is the salt here, and like all salts it is an ionic compound, which confirms ethanoic acid behaves as a typical acid. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Products: sodium ethanoate (the salt, an ionic compound) + water|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Ethanoic acid reacts with propanol, using concentrated sulfuric acid as the catalyst. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Ethanoic acid + propanol, with conc. sulfuric acid — what forms?|id=ex-q-1>> When these two react, they join together and lose a small molecule of water — so this is called a condensation reaction. The products are propyl ethanoate and water. <<WRITE_STEP:ethanoic acid + propanol → propyl ethanoate + water|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:CH_3COOH + C_3H_7OH \xrightarrow{\text{conc. } H_2SO_4} CH_3COOC_3H_7 + H_2O|id=ex-eq-1>> And the answer: the product is propyl ethanoate, which is an ester — and it smells of pears. Notice the reaction is reversible, and the sulfuric acid acts as a catalyst. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Propyl ethanoate (an ester, smells of pears) + water; reversible, sulfuric acid catalyst|id=ex-ans-1>> And because the molecules get heavier as the chain grows, look how <<TRACE:boiling-trend>> their boiling points climb steadily, from around one hundred one degrees Celsius for the smallest up to one hundred sixty four degrees for butanoic acid. So the next time vinegar makes your eyes water, remember it is <<FOCUS:carboxyl-group>> this one little carboxyl group doing the work, the same group hiding in every acid in the family. <<PAUSE:short>>

lesson_plans.title: Petroleum: The Ancient Fuel Made of Carbon Chains

hook.text: The petrol in a car engine today was once living creatures, swimming in an ocean millions of years before the dinosaurs even disappeared.

crucial_facts: Fossil fuels are the remains of ancient organisms, turned into fuel by millions of years of heat and pressure.
Petroleum is a mixture of hydrocarbons — molecules built only from carbon and hydrogen.

diagrams.purpose: Show that hydrocarbons are just carbon atoms linked in different shapes — chains and rings — each carbon surrounded by hydrogens.

required_elements.description: A straight chain of five carbon atoms bonded to each other, representing pentane, with each carbon bonded to hydrogen atoms filling its remaining bonds.
A ring of six carbon atoms bonded in a closed loop, representing cyclohexane, each carbon carrying hydrogen atoms.
A label pointing to one carbon atom in the chain, marked C for carbon.
A label pointing to a hydrogen atom attached to a carbon, marked H for hydrogen.

choreography.narration: The petrol burning in a car engine today was once living creatures, swimming in an ocean millions of years ago, long before the dinosaurs.
<<SECTION:Fossil fuels|id=sec-1>>When those tiny organisms died, they sank to the sea floor and got buried under thick layers of sediment, deeper and deeper, year after year.
Then, over millions of years, enormous pressure and heat slowly squeezed and cooked those buried remains into something new entirely.
That something is petroleum, also called crude oil — and along with coal and natural gas, it is what we call a fossil fuel, because it really is made from ancient fossils.
But here is the strange part: if you could smell a drop of crude oil, you would be smelling not one substance, but hundreds of different compounds all mixed together.
<<SECTION:Hydrocarbons|id=sec-2>>So what are all these compounds made of? Almost all of them are built from just two kinds of atom — carbon and hydrogen — and we call those molecules hydrocarbons.
Watch this chain take shape. Each grey atom here is carbon, the backbone of the whole molecule.
<<WRITE_TEXT:C = carbon, H = hydrogen|id=text-1>>This carbon, marked C, links to its neighbours, and every spare arm grabs a hydrogen atom, marked H. Carbon and hydrogen — that is the whole recipe.
Now, why hundreds of different compounds? Because carbon is a master builder — the same atoms can connect in a straight chain, or curl right around into a ring.
Short chains, long chains, rings, branches — each different shape is a different compound, which is exactly why crude oil is such a rich mixture.

<<WRITE_KEY:Petroleum = a mixture of hydrocarbons (carbon + hydrogen)|id=key-1>>So remember this: petroleum is not one chemical, it is a mixture of hydrocarbons, molecules made only from carbon and hydrogen.
And every time you fill a tank, you are burning carbon chains that took an ocean, a graveyard of ancient life, and millions of years of pressure to build.

lesson_plans.title: Refining Petroleum by Fractional Distillation

hook.text: Pump crude oil out of the ground and you don't get fuel — you get a thick black soup of hundreds of different molecules, all jumbled together and almost useless.

crucial_facts: Smaller, lighter hydrocarbon molecules boil off at low temperatures; bigger, heavier ones need much higher temperatures.
Fractional distillation sorts crude oil into useful fractions by separating molecules according to their boiling points.

diagrams.purpose: Show crude oil being heated and sorted into fractions by boiling point, with the temperature gradient making clear why small molecules separate first.

required_elements.description: A flame or heater at the bottom heating the crude oil flask.
Flask of dark crude oil being heated at the base of the apparatus.
Arrow showing hot vapours rising upward from the heated oil.
Vertical temperature scale running cool at the top to hot at the bottom, marked with example boiling temperatures.
Top collection point for the lightest, most volatile fraction (small molecules, low boiling point).
Bottom collection point for the heaviest fraction (large molecules, high boiling point).
Diagram of a small, short hydrocarbon molecule.
Diagram of a large, long hydrocarbon molecule.

choreography.narration: Pump crude oil out of the ground and you don't get fuel — you get a thick black soup of hundreds of different molecules, all jumbled together.

Every one of those molecules is a hydrocarbon — built only from hydrogen and carbon — but they come in wildly different sizes, from tiny short chains to enormous long ones. <<WRITE_TEXT:Crude oil = mixture of many hydrocarbons|id=text-1>>
A giant jumbled mixture like this is almost useless, so our first job is to sort it — and the trick is hiding in how these molecules behave when you heat them.
Here's the question: if I gently warm this whole mixture, which molecules do you think escape the liquid first?

The small, light ones. They're loosely held, so it takes only a little energy to free them — they boil off first, at low temperatures. The big heavy molecules cling on and need far more heat to escape. <<WRITE_KEY:Small molecules boil first (low temp); big molecules need high temp|id=key-1>>
So we heat the crude oil and let the vapours rise up through a tall column that's hot at the bottom and cool at the top.

As a vapour climbs and cools, it condenses back into a liquid the moment it reaches its own boiling temperature — and we collect it there. <<WRITE_TEXT:Vapour condenses where it cools to its boiling point|id=text-2>>
The lightest molecules stay as gas highest up and are caught at the cool top of the column.
The heaviest molecules barely rise at all — they condense low down where it's still scorching hot, and are drawn off at the bottom. <<SECTION:The fractions|id=sec-2>>
Because the lighter molecules boil at lower temperatures, each height in the column traps molecules of one particular size — that's exactly why the sorting works.

Here's an example from the chapter: refining petroleum in the lab. We gently heat the petroleum and let the compounds evaporate, collecting what condenses in cool test-tubes. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Refine petroleum by collecting fractions as the thermometer rises|id=ex-q-1>>

We start by watching what evaporates first. The smaller, lighter molecules go first, since it takes less energy to free them from the liquid. As the hot vapours rise, so does the thermometer reading. When the reading reaches one hundred degrees Celsius, we swap the first test-tube for an empty one, and that liquid is our first fraction. <<WRITE_STEP:Smaller lighter molecules evaporate first - swap first test-tube at 100 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-1>>

Then we collect three more fractions in the same way, swapping the test-tube at one hundred and fifty degrees Celsius, at two hundred degrees Celsius, and at three hundred degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Swap again at 150, 200, and 300 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-2>>

And the answer is that we end up with four fractions collected in total, each gathered over a rising temperature range. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Four fractions collected total, at 100, 150, 200, and 300 degrees Celsius|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. We're comparing four fractions collected from distillation, and we want to see how their properties change as the molecules get larger. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How do the four fractions compare in boiling point, runniness, volatility, and flammability?|id=ex-q-1>>

Let's lay them out in order. Fraction one boils up to one hundred degrees Celsius, it's very runny, very volatile, burns very easily, and it's made of small molecules. <<WRITE_STEP:Fraction 1: bp up to 100 C, very runny, volatile, burns very easily, small molecules|id=ex-step-1-1>> Fraction two boils between one hundred and one hundred fifty degrees Celsius, it's runny, less volatile, and burns easily. <<WRITE_STEP:Fraction 2: bp 100 to 150 C, runny, less volatile, burns easily|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Continuing down, fraction three boils between one hundred fifty and two hundred degrees Celsius, it's not very runny, even less volatile, and it does not burn easily. <<WRITE_STEP:Fraction 3: bp 150 to 200 C, not very runny, even less volatile, not easily burns|id=ex-step-1-3>> And fraction four boils between two hundred and three hundred degrees Celsius, it's viscous, thick and sticky, the least volatile, it only burns with a wick, and it's made of large molecules. <<WRITE_STEP:Fraction 4: bp 200 to 300 C, viscous, least volatile, burns only with a wick, large molecules|id=ex-step-1-4>>

So the pattern is clear: as the molecules get larger from fraction one through fraction four, the boiling point rises while runniness, volatility, and flammability all decrease together. <<WRITE_ANSWER:As molecules get larger (Fraction 1 to 4), boiling point rises; runniness, volatility, and flammability all decrease.|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. A fractional distillation tower separates crude oil by the size of the molecules. At the base it's over four hundred degrees Celsius, and near the top it's about twenty-five degrees Celsius. The bigger molecules condense low down where it's hot, and the smaller ones rise to the cooler top. Let's list the fractions from lightest to heaviest. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Name each refinery fraction by its carbon range and its use.|id=ex-q-1>>

We start at the top of the tower with the smallest molecules. Refinery gas has one to four carbon atoms and is used as bottled gas for cooking and heating. <<WRITE_STEP:Refinery gas: C1 to C4, cooking and heating gas|id=ex-step-1-1>> Next is gasoline, or petrol, with five to six carbon atoms, used as fuel for cars. <<WRITE_STEP:Gasoline (petrol): C5 to C6, car fuel|id=ex-step-1-2>> Then naphtha, six to ten carbon atoms, the feedstock for many chemicals and plastics. <<WRITE_STEP:Naphtha: C6 to C10, chemicals and plastics feedstock|id=ex-step-1-3>>

Moving down where it's warmer, paraffin, also called kerosene, has ten to fifteen carbon atoms and fuels aircraft and lamps. <<WRITE_STEP:Paraffin (kerosene): C10 to C15, aircraft and lamp fuel|id=ex-step-1-4>> Diesel oil has fifteen to twenty carbon atoms for diesel engines. <<WRITE_STEP:Diesel oil: C15 to C20, diesel engine fuel|id=ex-step-1-5>> Fuel oil has twenty to thirty carbon atoms for power stations and ships. <<WRITE_STEP:Fuel oil: C20 to C30, power stations and ships|id=ex-step-1-6>>

Finally, at the hot base of the tower, the heaviest molecules. The lubricating fraction has thirty to fifty carbon atoms, giving engine oil and waxes. <<WRITE_STEP:Lubricating fraction: C30 to C50, engine oil and waxes|id=ex-step-1-7>> And bitumen, with fifty carbon atoms upwards, is used for road surfaces and roofs. <<WRITE_STEP:Bitumen: C50 upwards, road surfaces and roofs|id=ex-step-1-8>> So the full set of fractions, from refinery gas at one to four carbon atoms up top, down to bitumen at fifty carbons and beyond at the base. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Eight fractions: refinery gas (C1-C4) to bitumen (C50+), heaviest at the hot base, lightest at the cool top|id=ex-ans-1>>

This whole process of separating crude oil into groups of similar-sized molecules has a name: fractional distillation, and the groups we collect are called fractions. <<WRITE_KEY:Fractional distillation sorts crude oil into fractions by boiling point|id=key-2>>

And that's the magic: one black useless soup goes in, and out come neat fractions — from runny, easily-burning fuels at the top to thick, heavy oils at the bottom — each one sorted purely by how easily its molecules let go of the liquid.

lesson_plans.title: Cracking: Breaking Big Molecules into Useful Ones

hook.text: Crude oil gives us far too much thick, heavy gloop that nobody wants to buy, and never enough of the light petrol that everyone is desperate for. So how do we turn the useless stuff into the valuable stuff?

crucial_facts: Cracking breaks large, less useful hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful ones using heat and a catalyst.
Cracking always produces an alkane and an alkene, and the alkene is what makes plastics possible.

diagrams.purpose: Show a long-chain hydrocarbon being broken at a bond into a shorter alkane and a double-bonded alkene, making the before-and-after obvious.

required_elements.description: A long zig-zag chain of about ten carbon atoms with hydrogens, representing the large heavy hydrocarbon reactant.
A marker on one carbon-carbon bond roughly in the middle of the long chain, showing where the chain snaps.
A short saturated chain product (all single bonds) drawn to the left after the split.
A short chain product with a carbon-carbon double bond drawn to the right after the split.
The carbon-carbon double bond inside the alkene product, highlighted to show the new reactive feature.

choreography.narration: Crude oil gives us far too much thick, heavy gloop that nobody wants, and never enough of the light petrol everyone is desperate for. So how do we turn the useless into the valuable?
<<SECTION:Cracking|id=sec-1>>Here is the heavy stuff: a hydrocarbon with a long chain of carbon atoms. Long chains mean a high boiling point, hard to set alight, not much use as a fuel.
Now imagine heating it really hard, and passing it over a hot catalyst. Something has to give. Where do you think this long chain will break?

<<WRITE_KEY:Cracking = breaking large hydrocarbons into smaller, more useful ones|id=key-1>>It snaps in the middle. The chain breaks into two smaller pieces, and that is cracking: breaking big molecules into smaller, more useful ones.
On this side we get a short chain where every carbon already holds all the hydrogen it can. We call that an alkane, and it is exactly the smaller, lighter fuel we wanted.
But here is the catch. When the chain snapped, this other piece was left short of hydrogen. Two of its carbons grab each other extra tightly instead.
<<WRITE_TEXT:alkene = has a C=C double bond|id=text-1>>That extra-tight grip is a double bond between two carbon atoms. A molecule with a carbon-to-carbon double bond is called an alkene.
Why should anyone care about that double bond? It looks like a small detail on the picture.

<<WRITE_KEY:Cracking makes an alkane AND an alkene; the alkene builds plastics|id=key-2>>Because that double bond is hungry to react. It lets thousands of alkene molecules link up into long chains, and those long chains are plastics. No cracking, no plastic.
So one big useless molecule becomes two prizes at once: a useful small fuel, and a reactive alkene for making materials.

Here's an example from the chapter. We take decane, with the formula C ten H twenty-two, which comes from the naphtha fraction. We heat it to five hundred and forty degrees Celsius with a catalyst, and it cracks into smaller molecules. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Crack decane (C10H22) from naphtha at 540 C with a catalyst|id=ex-q-1>>

We start by writing the reactant. One molecule of decane, C ten H twenty-two, contains ten carbon atoms and twenty-two hydrogen atoms. <<WRITE_STEP:Reactant: C10H22 (10 carbons, 22 hydrogens)|id=ex-step-1-1>>

Now we break it into three smaller molecules. It gives pentane, C five H twelve, which is suitable for petrol, plus propene, C three H six, plus ethene, C two H four. <<WRITE_STEP:Products: C5H12 + C3H6 + C2H4|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Let's check the atoms balance. On the product side the carbons are five plus three plus two, which makes ten carbons, matching the decane. The hydrogens are twelve plus six plus four, which makes twenty-two hydrogens, again matching. So ten carbons and twenty-two hydrogens split cleanly into three molecules. <<WRITE_STEP:Carbons: 5+3+2 = 10. Hydrogens: 12+6+4 = 22.|id=ex-step-1-3>>

Notice that propene and ethene each contain a carbon-to-carbon double bond. They belong to the alkene family, and that double bond makes them very reactive. <<WRITE_STEP:Propene and ethene are alkenes with C=C double bonds, very reactive|id=ex-step-1-4>>

And the answer is that decane has been broken down into three smaller molecules: pentane, suitable for petrol, plus the reactive alkenes propene and ethene. <<WRITE_ANSWER:C10H22 -> C5H12 + C3H6 + C2H4|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. Ethane has very short molecules, but even it can be cracked. We take ethane and pass it with steam at greater than eight hundred degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Crack ethane using steam at over 800 degrees Celsius. What forms?|id=ex-q-1>>

We start by breaking the ethane molecule apart under those harsh conditions. Cracking always pulls out a small reactive piece, leaving behind a molecule with a double bond. So ethane splits to give ethene plus hydrogen, that is, H two. <<WRITE_STEP:Ethane, with steam at greater than 800 degrees Celsius, gives ethene plus hydrogen (H2)|id=ex-step-1-1>>

And the answer is ethene and hydrogen. Notice we get that reactive double-bonded product, ethene, and the hydrogen produced can be used to make ammonia. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Products: ethene + hydrogen (H2); the hydrogen can be used to make ammonia|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. After crude oil is fractionally distilled, some of the fractions are still mixtures, so they get split further into individual compounds. Take the gas fraction as our case. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What does the gas fraction separate into?|id=ex-q-1>>
The gas fraction is separated into four individual compounds: methane, ethane, propane, and butane. <<WRITE_STEP:Gas fraction -> methane, ethane, propane, butane|id=ex-step-1-1>>

And here's the everyday connection: butane is the one we buy in canisters. So the gas fraction yields methane, ethane, propane, and butane, with butane sold in canisters. <<WRITE_ANSWER:methane, ethane, propane, butane (butane sold in canisters)|id=ex-ans-1>>
And because heat alone tore that strong molecule apart, chemists give cracking its proper name: thermal decomposition, breaking down using heat.

<<WRITE_EQUATION:C_{10}H_{22} \rightarrow C_{8}H_{18} + C_{2}H_{4}|id=eq-1>>In symbols, one large hydrocarbon arrow gives one smaller alkane plus one alkene. Count the atoms on each side and you will see nothing is lost, just rearranged.

equations.explanation_in_words: One large hydrocarbon breaks down into one smaller alkane plus one alkene, and every atom is conserved.

lesson_plans.title: Cracking the Code Hidden in Chemical Names

hook.text: There are over ten million known organic compounds — and yet you will never have to memorize a single name, because every name is secretly a code.

crucial_facts: The ENDING of an organic compound's name tells you its family (-ane, -ene, -ol, -oic acid).
The BEGINNING of the name tells you how many carbon atoms it has (meth- is one, eth- is two, prop- is three, but- is four).

diagrams.purpose: Show a compound name split into a prefix (carbon count) and a suffix (family), so the student literally sees the two pieces of the code.

required_elements.description: The whole word 'propanol' written large in the centre of the board.
The highlighted beginning 'prop-' of the name, coloured to stand out.
The highlighted ending '-ol' of the name, coloured differently to the prefix.
A simple chain of three carbon atoms drawn beneath the prefix, matching prop- equals three carbons.
A tag reading 'alcohol family' connected to the suffix part.

choreography.narration: There are more than ten million known organic compounds — and yet you will never have to memorize a single one of their names, because every name is secretly a code.
Here is the trick that chemists worked out: instead of inventing a random name for each compound, they built the name out of two clues stuck together.
<<SECTION:The hidden code|id=sec-1>>Look at this name on the board — propanol. It looks like one word, but it is really two pieces of information glued together.
The ending of the name — the very last part — tells you which family the compound belongs to.
If a name ends in -ane it is an alkane, if it ends in -ene it is an alkene, if it ends in -ol it is an alcohol, and if it ends in -oic acid it is a carboxylic acid.
So this ending, -ol, immediately tells me: this compound is a member of the alcohol family. I did not have to look anything up.
Now, the family alone is not enough — alcohols come in many sizes. So what tells me how big this particular molecule is?
The beginning of the name carries that second clue. <<WRITE_TEXT:prefix = carbon count|id=text-1>>The prefix tells you exactly how many carbon atoms are in the chain.
Meth- means one carbon, eth- means two, prop- means three, and but- means four. So prop- tells me this molecule has exactly three carbon atoms.
<<WRITE_KEY:Name = (how many carbons) + (which family)|id=key-1>>Put the two clues together and the name decodes itself: prop plus ol means a three-carbon molecule in the alcohol family.

Here's an example from the chapter. For the alkanes, the general formula is C n H two n plus two, where n is just a number that tells you how many carbon atoms are in the molecule. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Use the general formula CnH2n+2 to find the formulas of methane, ethane, and propane|id=ex-q-1>>

Let's start with methane. For methane, n is one. So we put one in for n, and two times one plus two gives four hydrogens. That's C one H four, which we write as CH four. <<WRITE_STEP:Methane: n = 1, so C1H(2x1+2) = CH4|id=ex-step-1-1>>
Next, ethane. For ethane, n is two. Two carbons, and two times two plus two gives six hydrogens. So that's C two H six. <<WRITE_STEP:Ethane: n = 2, so C2H(2x2+2) = C2H6|id=ex-step-1-2>>

And finally propane. For propane, n is three. Three carbons, and two times three plus two gives eight hydrogens. So that's C three H eight. <<WRITE_STEP:Propane: n = 3, so C3H(2x3+2) = C3H8|id=ex-step-1-3>>

And there are our answers: methane is CH four, ethane is C two H six, and propane is C three H eight, all built straight from the general formula C n H two n plus two. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Methane CH4, Ethane C2H6, Propane C3H8|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. Let's look at the first four members of the alkane family and watch what happens to their boiling points. Methane has one carbon atom, ethane has two carbon atoms, propane has three carbon atoms, and butane has four carbon atoms. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How does boiling point change from methane to butane?|id=ex-q-1>>

We start by listing each one with its boiling point. Methane, with just one carbon, has the lowest boiling point at about minus one hundred sixty-four degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Methane (1 C): about -164 degrees C|id=ex-step-1-1>> Ethane, with two carbons, boils a little higher. <<WRITE_STEP:Ethane (2 C): higher than methane|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Now we keep going up the chain. Propane, with three carbons, boils at about minus forty-two degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Propane (3 C): about -42 degrees C|id=ex-step-1-3>> And butane, with four carbons, boils at about minus zero point five degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Butane (4 C): about -0.5 degrees C|id=ex-step-1-4>>

Look at the pattern: each time we add a carbon, the boiling point climbs. So the answer is clear, the boiling point increases as the chain length increases. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Boiling point increases as chain length increases (methane < ethane < propane < butane)|id=ex-ans-1>>

And the simplest family of all, the alkanes, shows the pattern beautifully: methane has one carbon, ethane two, propane three, butane four — and as the chains get longer, the boiling points climb steadily upward.
So once you know the endings and the beginnings, you have not learned one compound — you have learned how to read millions of them at a glance.

lesson_plans.title: The Alkanes: Carbon's Simplest Family

hook.text: The gas that cooks your dinner, the fuel in a camping stove, the stuff inside a cigarette lighter — they're all from one family of molecules built from just two ingredients.

crucial_facts: Alkanes are hydrocarbons in which every carbon-to-carbon bond is a single bond, which makes them saturated.
Each member of the alkane family differs from the next by one carbon and two hydrogens, following the general formula C-n-H-two-n-plus-two.

diagrams.purpose: Show that an alkane is built only from carbon and hydrogen, and that the central carbon-to-carbon link is a single shared pair of electrons.

required_elements.description: A carbon atom on the left, labelled C.
A carbon atom on the right, labelled C.
The single bond between the two carbons, drawn as one shared pair of electrons (a single line).
The six hydrogen atoms, three bonded to each carbon, each labelled H.

choreography.narration: The gas that cooks your dinner, the fuel in a camping stove, the stuff inside a cigarette lighter, they all come from one single family of molecules built from just two ingredients.
<<SECTION:The Alkanes|id=sec-1>>Those two ingredients are carbon and hydrogen, and a molecule made of only carbon and hydrogen has a special name, a hydrocarbon.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Hydrocarbon = carbon + hydrogen only|id=text-1>>The alkanes are the simplest hydrocarbons of all, and the cleanest way to meet them is to look at one molecule up close.
Here is ethane, and you can see its skeleton is just two carbon atoms, with hydrogen atoms hanging off the outside, nothing else in the whole molecule.
Now look right at the middle, at the link joining the two carbons together.
That link is one shared pair of electrons, and one shared pair is exactly what we mean by a single bond.

<<WRITE_KEY:Every C-C bond is single, so alkanes are saturated|id=key-1>>And this is the rule for the whole family: every carbon-to-carbon bond is a single bond, with no spare bonds left over, which is why we call the alkanes saturated.
<<SECTION:A family with a pattern|id=sec-2>>The alkanes aren't just one molecule though, they're a whole series, and the series follows a beautifully simple pattern.
Start with methane, one carbon. Add a carbon and two hydrogens and you get ethane. Add another carbon and two more hydrogens and you get propane.
So if I just told you a molecule has ten carbons, could you tell me exactly how many hydrogens it must have, without ever seeing it?

<<WRITE_KEY:Each step: +1 carbon, +2 hydrogens|id=key-2>>Yes, you can, because each member differs from the next by one carbon and two hydrogens, and that locks in the formula carbon-n hydrogen two-n-plus-two.

Here's an example from the chapter. When methane burns in a good supply of oxygen, it undergoes complete combustion. We start with one molecule of methane, that's C H four, reacting with two molecules of oxygen, two O two. The reaction needs that good supply of oxygen to burn cleanly. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What is the complete combustion of methane?|id=ex-q-1>>

Now we write the reactants on the left. One methane molecule plus two oxygen molecules. <<WRITE_STEP:Reactants: one C H four plus two O two|id=ex-step-1-1>><<WRITE_EQUATION:CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow|id=ex-eq-1>>

These react together to form the products. One molecule of methane gives one carbon dioxide, that's one C O two, plus two molecules of water, two H two O, and it releases plenty of heat energy. So the answer is: C H four plus two O two gives one C O two plus two H two O plus heat energy. <<WRITE_ANSWER:CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O + heat energy|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. When there isn't enough oxygen, alkanes undergo incomplete combustion, and instead of carbon dioxide they produce poisonous carbon monoxide. Let's balance the equation for methane burning in too little oxygen. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Write the incomplete combustion of methane in insufficient oxygen|id=ex-q-1>>

We start on the left side with two molecules of methane reacting with three molecules of oxygen. Because there isn't enough oxygen, the carbon can't fully oxidise. <<WRITE_STEP:2 CH4 + 3 O2 -> ?|id=ex-step-1-1>>

Working out the products: the carbon ends up as carbon monoxide, so we get two molecules of carbon monoxide, and the hydrogen forms four molecules of water. And critically, this reaction releases less heat energy than complete combustion, all because there is not enough oxygen. <<WRITE_STEP:Products: 2 CO + 4 H2O + less heat|id=ex-step-1-2>>

And the answer is the balanced equation: two methane plus three oxygen gives two carbon monoxide plus four water, releasing less heat energy. <<WRITE_ANSWER:2 CH4 (g) + 3 O2 (g) -> 2 CO (g) + 4 H2O (l) + less heat energy|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. Methane reacts with chlorine, that's C-l-two, but only in sunlight. The light is essential because it breaks the chlorine bonds, so this is a photochemical reaction. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What happens when methane reacts with chlorine in sunlight?|id=ex-q-1>>

We start with the first reaction. In sunlight, methane plus chlorine produces chloromethane, C-H-three-C-l, plus hydrogen chloride, H-C-l. We call this a substitution reaction, because a chlorine atom takes the place of a hydrogen atom. <<WRITE_STEP:methane + Cl2 --(light)--> chloromethane (CH3Cl) + HCl|id=ex-step-1-1>>

And if there's enough chlorine, all four hydrogen atoms get replaced, one by one, giving a whole series: chloromethane C-H-three-C-l, then dichloromethane C-H-two-C-l-two, then trichloromethane C-H-C-l-three, and finally tetrachloromethane C-C-l-four. <<WRITE_ANSWER:CH3Cl, then CH2Cl2, then CHCl3, then CCl4|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. Take two alkanes that share the exact same formula, C four H ten. The first is butane, which has a straight, unbranched chain. The second is two-methylpropane, where the chain is branched. They're isomers — same formula, different structure. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Butane and 2-methylpropane both have formula C4H10. Compare their boiling points.|id=ex-q-1>>

Let's compare their boiling points. Butane, the straight-chain molecule, boils at zero degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Butane (straight chain): boiling point = 0 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-1>> The branched one, two-methylpropane, boils at minus ten degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:2-methylpropane (branched): boiling point = -10 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-2>> So the branched isomer has the lower boiling point. <<WRITE_STEP:Branched isomer has the lower boiling point|id=ex-step-1-3>>

Why? Because branching reduces the attraction between molecules — the branches make it harder for the molecules to get close to each other, so less energy is needed to pull them apart. That's the takeaway: the branched isomer, two-methylpropane, boils lower at minus ten degrees Celsius, because branching reduces attraction between molecules. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Branched 2-methylpropane boils lower (-10 degrees Celsius vs 0 degrees Celsius for butane), because branching reduces attraction between molecules.|id=ex-ans-1>>

<<WRITE_STEP:Ten carbons: 2 times 10 plus 2 = 22 hydrogens|id=step-1>>For ten carbons, two times ten plus two gives twenty-two hydrogens, so the molecule is carbon ten hydrogen twenty-two, and you never had to draw it.
So a family built from only carbon and hydrogen, joined entirely by single bonds, marching up in steps of one carbon and two hydrogens, that, in one breath, is what an alkane is.

equations.explanation_in_words: Because each member differs from the next by one carbon and two hydrogens, the number of hydrogens is always two times the number of carbons, plus two more.

lesson_plans.title: The Alkenes: The Family with a Double Bond

hook.text: What if a single tiny change in how two carbon atoms hold hands could turn one chemical family into a completely different, far more reactive one?

crucial_facts: Every alkene contains a carbon-to-carbon double bond, which is its reactive functional group and makes the molecule unsaturated.
Alkenes follow the general formula C n H 2 n, so the number of hydrogen atoms is always exactly twice the number of carbon atoms.

diagrams.purpose: Show the carbon-to-carbon double bond at the heart of every alkene, contrasting the two shared pairs against single bonds, so the functional group is visible.

required_elements.description: Left carbon atom labelled C
Right carbon atom labelled C
The two parallel lines between the two carbon atoms representing the carbon-to-carbon double bond
The four hydrogen atoms, two attached to each carbon, each joined by a single bond

choreography.narration: What if one tiny change in how two carbon atoms hold hands could turn an ordinary, sleepy chemical into a far more reactive one?

Meet the alkenes, a family of compounds built from only two elements, carbon and hydrogen. <<SECTION:The alkene family|id=sec-1>>Because they contain only those two elements, we call them hydrocarbons.
Here is the simplest alkene, called ethene. Two carbon atoms sitting in the middle, with hydrogen atoms hanging off the sides.
Now look right here, between the two carbons. There are not one but two lines joining them. That is a carbon-to-carbon double bond, two shared pairs of electrons instead of one.

<<WRITE_KEY:Every alkene has a C=C double bond, its functional group|id=key-1>>This double bond is the single most important feature of the whole family. It is their functional group, the part that decides how they react.

Because that double bond is sitting there ready to open up and grab onto other atoms, we say alkenes are unsaturated. <<WRITE_TEXT:C=C present means unsaturated|id=text-1>>An alkane, with only single bonds, is full up, or saturated.
So that double bond is what makes alkenes special. But how do all the members of this family relate to one another?
They form a homologous series, which is just a fancy name for a family where each member follows the same pattern and differs from the next by a fixed building block.
<<SECTION:The general formula|id=sec-2>>And that pattern is beautifully simple. In every alkene, the number of hydrogen atoms is always exactly twice the number of carbon atoms.
<<WRITE_KEY:Alkenes: C n H 2 n|id=key-2>>We write that as the general formula C n H two n. So if you tell me there are three carbons, I instantly know there are six hydrogens.
Watch it work. Ethene has two carbons, so four hydrogens. Propene has three carbons, so six hydrogens. Each step adds one carbon and two hydrogens, the same building block every time.
So remember the two big ideas: every alkene carries that reactive carbon-to-carbon double bond, and they all obey the formula C n H two n. Know the carbons, and the hydrogens fall right out.

equations.explanation_in_words: The number of hydrogen atoms is always exactly twice the number of carbon atoms.

lesson_plans.title: Alkenes and the C-n-H-2n Formula: The Double-Bond Doorway

hook.text: Here are two molecules. One will sit in a jar for years doing nothing. The other will grab onto almost anything you throw at it. They are built from the same two ingredients, carbon and hydrogen. So what makes one a couch potato and the other a magnet?

crucial_facts: Every alkene fits the general formula C-n-H-2-n because the carbon-carbon double bond costs the molecule one pair of hydrogen atoms compared with the matching alkane.
Alkenes are reactive because that double bond can open up and add atoms on, which is exactly what makes a molecule unsaturated.

diagrams.purpose: Show ethene's carbon-carbon double bond beside ethane's single bond so the student can literally count the missing pair of hydrogens and see why the formula is C-n-H-2-n.

required_elements.description: The carbon-to-carbon double bond at the centre of an ethene molecule, drawn as two parallel lines between the two carbon atoms.
Left carbon atom of ethene with its two attached hydrogen atoms.
Right carbon atom of ethene with its two attached hydrogen atoms.
The four hydrogen atoms of ethene, two on each carbon.
The single carbon-to-carbon bond of ethane drawn beside ethene for comparison.
The two extra hydrogen atoms ethane has that ethene lacks, highlighted to show the difference.

choreography.narration: Here are two molecules. One sits in a jar for years doing nothing; the other grabs onto almost anything you throw at it. Same two ingredients, carbon and hydrogen, so what makes the difference?
Look right at the centre of this molecule. The two carbon atoms are joined not by one line, but by two. That is a double bond, and it is the entire story of the alkenes.
<<SECTION:Counting the hydrogens|id=sec-1>>Now let us count. This molecule is ethene. Each carbon holds two hydrogen atoms, so four hydrogens in total around two carbons.
Beside it is ethane, the lazy one. Its carbons are joined by a single bond, and look, it has room for two extra hydrogen atoms that ethene simply does not have.
So why does an alkene always have exactly twice as many hydrogens as carbons, the pattern we write as C-n-H-2-n?
Because making that second bond between the carbons uses up a pair of hands that would otherwise hold hydrogens. The double bond literally costs the molecule one pair of hydrogen atoms.

<<WRITE_KEY:Every alkene fits C-n-H-2-n because the double bond costs one pair of hydrogens|id=key-1>>That is why every member of the family, two carbons, three carbons, ten carbons, always lands on twice as many hydrogens as carbons. The formula is C-n-H-2-n, and now you can see exactly where it comes from.

<<SECTION:Why alkenes are so reactive|id=sec-2>>Now here is the beautiful part. Picture that double bond as a doorway. One of the two bonds can swing open, leaving each carbon with a free hand ready to grab a new atom.

<<WRITE_TEXT:double bond opens, atoms add on|id=text-1>>When that doorway opens and new atoms attach, we call it an addition reaction. Ethene can add hydrogen back on to become ethane, or add water to become ethanol.

Here's an example from the chapter. We make alkenes from alkanes by a process called cracking. In this case, our starting material is ethane, and we pass it together with steam over a catalyst at a temperature of over eight hundred degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Crack ethane with steam at over 800 C — what forms?|id=ex-q-1>>

When we crack ethane under these conditions, the molecule breaks apart. The carbon chain rearranges to form a carbon-to-carbon double bond, giving us ethene, and at the same time a molecule of hydrogen is released. <<WRITE_STEP:ethane + steam, over 800 C → cracking|id=ex-step-1-1>>
So the products are ethene and hydrogen. Ethane, with steam at over eight hundred degrees Celsius, gives ethene plus hydrogen. <<WRITE_ANSWER:ethane → ethene + hydrogen|id=ex-ans-1>>
Here's an example from the chapter. Ethene, which is a gas, reacts with hydrogen gas in an addition reaction. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What does ethene form when it reacts with hydrogen?|id=ex-q-1>>

For this reaction to happen, we need a catalyst, along with heat and pressure. Under those conditions, the hydrogen adds across the double bond of ethene. <<WRITE_STEP:Ethene (gas) + hydrogen gas, with a catalyst, heat and pressure|id=ex-step-1-1>>
The product is ethane gas, a saturated molecule. So the answer is: ethene plus hydrogen gives ethane gas. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Ethene + H2 -> ethane (gas)|id=ex-ans-1>>
Here's an example from the chapter. Ethene, which is a gas, reacts with water in the form of steam. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What does ethene form when it adds water across its double bond?|id=ex-q-1>>

For this reaction to happen, we need a catalyst, along with heat and pressure. Under those conditions, ethene adds water across its double bond. <<WRITE_STEP:Ethene (gas) plus water as steam, with a catalyst, heat and pressure|id=ex-step-1>>
And the product is ethanol, a liquid alcohol. <<WRITE_ANSWER:The product is ethanol, a liquid alcohol|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. Take ethene as our starting molecule, the monomer, and let it undergo polymerisation. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Many ethene monomers join by polymerisation — what forms?|id=ex-q-1>>

We start by joining many ethene molecules together. Each ethene monomer links to the next, opening its double bond so the units chain end to end. <<WRITE_STEP:Step 1: Many ethene monomers (the monomer) join by polymerisation.|id=ex-step-1-1>>

And the answer is that the product is poly of ethene, also called polythene, and this chain can be many thousands of carbon atoms long. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Product = poly(ethene) / polythene — chains many thousands of carbon atoms long.|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. Bromine water is an orange solution, and we use it to test whether a hydrocarbon is unsaturated. Take ethene, which is a gas, and bubble it through this orange bromine water. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What happens when ethene gas is bubbled through orange bromine water?|id=ex-q-1>>

Ethene has a carbon-carbon double bond, so it reacts with bromine water in an addition reaction. The bromine adds straight across that double bond. <<WRITE_STEP:ethene (gas) + bromine water (orange) gives an addition reaction|id=ex-step-1-1>>

The product is one-two-dibromoethane, which is colourless, so the orange colour disappears. <<WRITE_ANSWER:ethene + bromine water gives 1,2-dibromoethane (colourless) — the orange colour disappears|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. We're asked to compare three compounds that all share the very same molecular formula, C four H eight. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Three compounds all have formula C4H8 but different structures. What are they?|id=ex-q-1>>

So all three have formula C four H eight, but when we draw them out we find they have different structures and the double bond sits in different positions. That tells us straight away these are isomers of one another. <<WRITE_STEP:Same formula C4H8, different structures and double-bond positions -> isomers|id=ex-step-1>>

And the answer is that the three isomers are but-one-ene, but-two-ene, and two-methylpropene, all members of the alkene family. <<WRITE_ANSWER:The three C4H8 isomers are but-1-ene, but-2-ene and 2-methylpropene|id=ex-ans-1>>
A molecule with a double bond waiting to open is called unsaturated. Once it has grabbed its extra atoms and the doorway is shut, it is saturated, just like the lazy alkane next door.

So that is the whole secret. The double bond costs an alkene one pair of hydrogens, giving the formula C-n-H-2-n, and that same double bond is the open doorway that makes alkenes far more reactive than alkanes.

equations.explanation_in_words: For an alkene with any number of carbons, you always get exactly twice as many hydrogen atoms as carbon atoms.

lesson_plans.title: The Alcohols: A Family Built on One Group

hook.text: The same stuff that fuels some cars, dissolves the scent in your perfume, and sits in alcoholic drinks is one single molecule — and it belongs to a family you can recognise by one tiny tag of just two atoms.

crucial_facts: An alcohol is any organic compound carrying the O-H group bonded to a carbon chain — that group is what makes it an alcohol.
The alcohols form a homologous series with general formula C n H two n plus one O H, so each member differs from the last by one C H two unit and properties change in a steady, predictable way.

diagrams.purpose: Show the O-H functional group staying constant while the carbon chain grows by one carbon each step, making the homologous pattern visible.

required_elements.description: The oxygen-hydrogen (O-H) group drawn at the right-hand end, highlighted as the constant tag shared by every member.
The chain of carbon atoms with their hydrogens, starting at one carbon (methanol) and extending as more carbons are added.
Full structural formula of methanol: one carbon with three hydrogens bonded to an O-H group.
Full structural formula of ethanol: two carbons in a chain ending in the O-H group.
The extra C H two unit that gets inserted into the chain when moving from one member to the next, highlighted to show the repeating pattern.

choreography.narration: The same stuff that fuels some cars, dissolves the scent in your perfume, and sits in alcoholic drinks is one single molecule — and it belongs to a family you can spot by one tiny tag of just two atoms.
<<SECTION:What makes an alcohol?|id=sec-1>>Look at this little group right here: an oxygen joined to a hydrogen. We call it the O-H group, and it is the secret handshake of the entire family.
Whenever you see that O-H group hanging off a carbon chain, you are looking at an alcohol — full stop. <<WRITE_TEXT:O-H group on a carbon chain = alcohol|id=text-1>>
Here is the smallest one possible: a single carbon, wearing its hydrogens, with that O-H group on the end. This is methanol.
Now watch what happens when I add just one more carbon to the chain. The O-H group stays exactly where it is — it never changes.
What we have built now is ethanol, the alcohol in drinks and in that perfume solvent. Notice nothing important changed except the chain got one carbon longer.
So if every single member is just a chain of carbons with their hydrogens, capped by the same O-H group, could we write one formula that describes the whole family at once?

<<SECTION:One pattern for the whole family|id=sec-2>>We can. For n carbon atoms you get n carbons, two n plus one hydrogens, and the O-H. That is why we call them a homologous series — a family that follows a regular, predictable pattern. <<WRITE_KEY:General formula: C n H two n plus one O H|id=key-1>>

And because each step adds exactly one carbon and two hydrogens, the properties march along in step too. The boiling points climb steadily as the chains get longer — from sixty-five degrees Celsius, to seventy-eight, to eighty-seven, to one hundred seventeen.

Here's an example from the chapter on making ethanol the biological way. We start with glucose, that's C six H twelve O six, in aqueous solution. Using yeast, the reaction is carried out in the absence of air, and it turns that glucose into ethanol. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How is ethanol made from glucose by fermentation?|id=ex-q-1>>

Now, yeast is a mass of living cells, and the enzymes inside it catalyse the reaction. One molecule of glucose breaks down to produce two molecules of ethanol, that's C two H five O H, and two molecules of carbon dioxide, C O two. Let's write that equation down. <<WRITE_STEP:Glucose C6H12O6 (aq) -> 2 C2H5OH (aq) + 2 CO2 (g) + energy|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:C_6H_{12}O_6\,(aq) \rightarrow 2\,C_2H_5OH\,(aq) + 2\,CO_2\,(g) + \text{energy}|id=ex-eq-1>>

Notice that the reaction also releases energy, so it is exothermic. This whole process is called fermentation. Finally, the ethanol is separated from the mixture by fractional distillation. So the answer: glucose ferments to give two molecules of ethanol plus two molecules of carbon dioxide plus energy, then the ethanol is recovered by fractional distillation. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Fermentation: C6H12O6 -> 2 C2H5OH + 2 CO2 + energy; ethanol separated by fractional distillation|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. We want to make ethanol the chemical way, by the hydration of ethene. Hydration means water is added on, so this is an addition reaction where ethene, C two H four, reacts with water, H two O. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How is ethanol made by hydration of ethene?|id=ex-q-1>>

We start by writing the reaction. Ethene gas plus water vapour gives ethanol, a liquid. This is carried out at a temperature of five hundred and seventy degrees Celsius and a pressure of sixty to seventy atmospheres, using a catalyst of phosphoric acid. <<WRITE_STEP:C2H4 (g) + H2O (g) -> C2H5OH (l)|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Conditions: 570 degrees C, 60-70 atm, phosphoric acid catalyst|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Now notice the reaction is reversible and exothermic. In theory, high pressure and a low temperature would give the best yield. But in practice a high temperature of five hundred and seventy degrees Celsius is used to give a good rate of reaction, and the phosphoric acid catalyst speeds it up further. So the answer is: ethanol is made by adding water to ethene at five hundred and seventy degrees Celsius and sixty to seventy atmospheres over a phosphoric acid catalyst, in a reversible, exothermic addition reaction. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Ethanol made by hydration of ethene: C2H4 + H2O -> C2H5OH, at 570 C, 60-70 atm, phosphoric acid catalyst (reversible, exothermic)|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. We take one molecule of liquid ethanol, C two H five O H, and burn it in oxygen. The question is: what does it produce, and why does that make it a good fuel? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Combustion of ethanol in oxygen|id=ex-q-1>>
We start by writing the reactants. One molecule of ethanol reacts with three molecules of oxygen, O two. <<WRITE_STEP:C2H5OH (l) + 3 O2 (g) -> ...|id=ex-step-1-1>>

Now we balance the products. The carbons go into carbon dioxide, giving two molecules of carbon dioxide, C O two, and the hydrogens go into water, giving three molecules of liquid water, H two O. Crucially, the reaction also releases heat. <<WRITE_STEP:... -> 2 CO2 (g) + 3 H2O (l) + heat|id=ex-step-1-2>>

And so the answer is: one molecule of ethanol plus three molecules of oxygen gives two molecules of carbon dioxide, three molecules of water, and heat. That released heat is exactly why ethanol works as a fuel. <<WRITE_ANSWER:C2H5OH (l) + 3 O2 (g) -> 2 CO2 (g) + 3 H2O (l) + heat|id=ex-ans-1>>

This is the real power of a homologous series: meet one member and understand its O-H group, and you can predict how every cousin in the family behaves. <<WRITE_TEXT:same O-H group = similar reactions|id=text-2>>
So remember the one idea that unlocks all of organic chemistry's families: find the functional group — for alcohols that is the O-H — and you have found what the whole family has in common.

equations.explanation_in_words: Because every member is just a chain of n carbons with their hydrogens, capped by the O-H group, we can write one formula that covers the whole family at once.

lesson_plans.title: The Carboxylic Acids: The Family Behind Vinegar

hook.text: That sour sting in your vinegar, the tang in sour milk, the bite of a stinging nettle, they all come from the same little cluster of atoms.

crucial_facts: Every carboxylic acid contains the same carboxyl group, C-O-O-H, and that group is what gives the whole family its shared behaviour.
The carboxylic acids form a homologous series with general formula C n H two n O two, so each member differs from the next by just one carbon atom.

diagrams.purpose: Show that all four simplest carboxylic acids share the identical carboxyl group while their carbon chains grow one atom at a time.

required_elements.description: The C-O-O-H carboxyl group: a carbon double-bonded to one oxygen and single-bonded to an O-H, drawn highlighted as the shared feature across all members.
Structural formula of methanoic acid, HCOOH, with one carbon, the H attached to the carboxyl carbon.
Structural formula of ethanoic acid, CH3COOH, showing a two-carbon chain ending in the carboxyl group.
Label bracketing the growing hydrocarbon chain portion that changes from member to member, separate from the fixed carboxyl group.
A small ladder or arrow noting boiling points rising from about one hundred one degrees to one hundred sixty four degrees as chain length grows.

choreography.narration: That sour sting in your vinegar, the tang in sour milk, the bite of a stinging nettle, they all come from the same little cluster of atoms.
<<SECTION:The carboxyl group|id=sec-1>>This cluster is a carbon joined to two oxygens in a special way, one by a double bond and one carrying a hydrogen, and we write it as C-O-O-H.
<<WRITE_TEXT:C-O-O-H = the carboxyl group|id=text-1>>Wherever you find this group, you have a carboxylic acid, an organic acid, and we call this group the carboxyl group.
Here is the simplest one of all, methanoic acid, just a single carbon wearing that carboxyl group.
Now watch what happens when we add one more carbon: we get ethanoic acid, the acid that makes vinegar sour, and notice the carboxyl group on the end has not changed at all.
<<WRITE_TEXT:chain grows, carboxyl group stays|id=text-2>>So here is the pattern of the whole family: only the carbon chain grows, one atom at a time, while this same group stays bolted on the end.
If only the chain length changes, could we capture every single member with one tidy formula?

<<WRITE_KEY:General formula C n H two n O two|id=key-1>>Yes we can, and here it is: C n H two n O two, where n is just the number of carbons, two oxygens always, because that is the carboxyl group counted in.
A family like this, where each member differs from the next by one carbon and they all obey one general formula, is called a homologous series.

Here's an example from the chapter. The carboxylic acids form a homologous series with the general formula C n H two n O two, and every member carries the same functional group, COOH, the carboxyl group. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Show how the boiling points of the carboxylic acids change as the molecules get bigger.|id=ex-q-1>>

Let's line up the first four members by their number of carbon atoms and read off their boiling points. Methanoic acid has one carbon atom and boils at one hundred and one degrees Celsius. Ethanoic acid has two carbon atoms and boils at one hundred and eighteen degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Methanoic acid, 1 carbon, boiling point 101 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Ethanoic acid, 2 carbons, boiling point 118 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Now the next two. Propanoic acid has three carbon atoms and boils at one hundred and forty-one degrees Celsius, and butanoic acid has four carbon atoms and boils at one hundred and sixty-four degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Propanoic acid, 3 carbons, boiling point 141 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<WRITE_STEP:Butanoic acid, 4 carbons, boiling point 164 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-4>>

So as the molecules get bigger, from one carbon up to four carbons, the boiling point climbs steadily, from one hundred and one degrees Celsius all the way up to one hundred and sixty-four degrees Celsius. The boiling points of the carboxylic acids rise as the molecules get bigger. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Boiling points rise with size: 101, 118, 141, 164 degrees Celsius for 1 to 4 carbons|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. We oxidise ethanol much faster by warming it with a powerful oxidising agent, potassium manganate seven, in the presence of acid. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Oxidise ethanol to ethanoic acid using potassium manganate(VII) in acid — what is the colour change?|id=ex-q-1>>

The manganate seven ions are themselves reduced to Mn two plus ions, and the acid provides the H plus ions for the reaction. <<WRITE_STEP:Acid provides H+ ions for the reaction|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:MnO_4^- + 8H^+ + 5e^- \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O|id=ex-eq-1>>

So the colour change tells us it has worked: with potassium manganate seven the colour goes from purple to colourless. And potassium dichromate six could be used as an alternative oxidising agent, giving a colour change from orange to green. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Potassium manganate(VII): purple → colourless. Alternative — potassium dichromate(VI): orange → green.|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. We're looking at a solution of ethanoic acid in water, and we want to understand why it behaves the way it does. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Why is ethanoic acid a weak acid?|id=ex-q-1>>

When ethanoic acid is put in water, some of its molecules dissociate. Each molecule that dissociates splits into an ethanoate ion and a hydrogen ion. So ethanoic acid breaks apart into ethanoate ions plus hydrogen ions. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\mathrm{CH_3COOH\,(aq) \rightarrow CH_3COO^-\,(aq) + H^+\,(aq)}|id=ex-eq-1>>

Now here's the key point. Only some of the molecules dissociate in this way, not all of them. Because only some molecules dissociate, ethanoic acid is a weak acid. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Ethanoic acid is a weak acid because only some of its molecules dissociate into ethanoate ions and hydrogen ions.|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. Ethanoic acid reacts with sodium hydroxide, and we want to see why this shows ethanoic acid is a typical acid. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What happens when ethanoic acid reacts with sodium hydroxide?|id=ex-q-1>>

We start by recognising the pattern. Sodium hydroxide is a base, and acids react with bases to form a salt plus water. So ethanoic acid plus sodium hydroxide gives sodium ethanoate plus water. <<WRITE_STEP:ethanoic acid + sodium hydroxide -> sodium ethanoate + water|id=ex-step-1-1>><<WRITE_EQUATION:CH_3COOH\,(aq) + NaOH\,(aq) \rightarrow CH_3COONa\,(aq) + H_2O\,(l)|id=ex-eq-1>>

And the answer is that the products are sodium ethanoate and water. Sodium ethanoate is the salt here, and like all salts it is an ionic compound, which confirms ethanoic acid behaves as a typical acid. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Products: sodium ethanoate (the salt, an ionic compound) + water|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. Ethanoic acid reacts with propanol, using concentrated sulfuric acid as the catalyst. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Ethanoic acid + propanol, with conc. sulfuric acid — what forms?|id=ex-q-1>>

When these two react, they join together and lose a small molecule of water — so this is called a condensation reaction. The products are propyl ethanoate and water. <<WRITE_STEP:ethanoic acid + propanol → propyl ethanoate + water|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:CH_3COOH + C_3H_7OH \xrightarrow{\text{conc. } H_2SO_4} CH_3COOC_3H_7 + H_2O|id=ex-eq-1>>

And the answer: the product is propyl ethanoate, which is an ester — and it smells of pears. Notice the reaction is reversible, and the sulfuric acid acts as a catalyst. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Propyl ethanoate (an ester, smells of pears) + water; reversible, sulfuric acid catalyst|id=ex-ans-1>>

And because the molecules get heavier as the chain grows, look how their boiling points climb steadily, from around one hundred one degrees Celsius for the smallest up to one hundred sixty four degrees for butanoic acid.
So the next time vinegar makes your eyes water, remember it is this one little carboxyl group doing the work, the same group hiding in every acid in the family.

equations.explanation_in_words: Because every member is just a carboxyl group with a growing carbon chain, we can write one formula that fits them all: take any number of carbons n, give it twice as many hydrogens, and exactly two oxygens.

segments.text_with_markers: Every one of those molecules is a hydrocarbon — built only from hydrogen and carbon — but they come in wildly different sizes, from tiny short chains to enormous long ones. <<WRITE_TEXT:Crude oil = mixture of many hydrocarbons|id=text-1>> <<POINT:small-molecule>>

segments.raw_narration: A giant jumbled mixture like this is almost useless, so our first job is to sort it — and the trick is hiding in how these molecules behave when you heat them.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:large-molecule>> A giant jumbled mixture like this is almost useless, so our first job is to sort it — and the trick is hiding in how these molecules behave when you heat them.

segments.raw_narration: Here's the question: if I gently warm this whole mixture, which molecules do you think escape the liquid first?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:heat-source>> Here's the question: if I gently warm this whole mixture, which molecules do you think escape the liquid first? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: The small, light ones. They're loosely held, so it takes only a little energy to free them — they boil off first, at low temperatures. segments.raw_narration: So we heat the crude oil and let the vapours rise up through a tall column that's hot at the bottom and cool at the top.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:rising-vapour>> So we heat the crude oil and let the vapours rise up through a tall column that's hot at the bottom and cool at the top. <<TRACE:rising-vapour>>

segments.raw_narration: As a vapour climbs and cools, it condenses back into a liquid the moment it reaches its own boiling temperature — and we collect it there. <<WRITE_TEXT:Vapour condenses where it cools to its boiling point|id=text-2>>
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:temperature-scale>> As a vapour climbs and cools, it condenses back into a liquid the moment it reaches its own boiling temperature — and we collect it there. <<WRITE_TEXT:Vapour condenses where it cools to its boiling point|id=text-2>>

segments.raw_narration: The lightest molecules stay as gas highest up and are caught at the cool top of the column.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:fraction-light>> The lightest molecules stay as gas highest up and are caught at the cool top of the column.

segments.raw_narration: The heaviest molecules barely rise at all — they condense low down where it's still scorching hot, and are drawn off at the bottom. <<SECTION:The fractions|id=sec-2>>
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:fraction-heavy>> The heaviest molecules barely rise at all — they condense low down where it's still scorching hot, and are drawn off at the bottom. <<SECTION:The fractions|id=sec-2>>

segments.raw_narration: Because the lighter molecules boil at lower temperatures, each height in the column traps molecules of one particular size — that's exactly why the sorting works.

Fraction one boils up to one hundred degrees Celsius, it's very runny, very volatile, burns very easily, and it's made of small molecules. <<WRITE_STEP:Fraction 1: bp up to 100 C, very runny, volatile, burns very easily, small molecules|id=ex-step-1-1>> Fraction two boils between one hundred and one hundred fifty degrees Celsius, it's runny, less volatile, and burns easily. <<WRITE_STEP:Fraction 2: bp 100 to 150 C, runny, less volatile, burns easily|id=ex-step-1-2>>

segments.raw_narration: There are more than ten million known organic compounds — and yet you will never have to memorize a single one of their names, because every name is secretly a code.
segments.text_with_markers: There are more than ten million known organic compounds — and yet you will never have to memorize a single one of their names, because every name is secretly a code.

segments.raw_narration: Here is the trick that chemists worked out: instead of inventing a random name for each compound, they built the name out of two clues stuck together.
segments.text_with_markers: Here is the trick that chemists worked out: instead of inventing a random name for each compound, they built the name out of two clues stuck together.

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:The hidden code|id=sec-1>>Look at this name on the board — propanol. It looks like one word, but it is really two pieces of information glued together.

segments.raw_narration: The ending of the name — the very last part — tells you which family the compound belongs to.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:suffix-part>> The ending of the name — the very last part — tells you which family the compound belongs to. <<POINT:suffix-part>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: If a name ends in -ane it is an alkane, if it ends in -ene it is an alkene, if it ends in -ol it is an alcohol, and if it ends in -oic acid it is a carboxylic acid.
segments.text_with_markers: If a name ends in -ane it is an alkane, if it ends in -ene it is an alkene, if it ends in -ol it is an alcohol, and if it ends in -oic acid it is a carboxylic acid. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: So this ending, -ol, immediately tells me: this compound is a member of the alcohol family. I did not have to look anything up.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:family-tag>> So this ending, -ol, immediately tells me: this compound is a member of the alcohol family. I did not have to look anything up.

segments.raw_narration: Now, the family alone is not enough — alcohols come in many sizes. So what tells me how big this particular molecule is?
