segments.raw_narration: The beginning of the name carries that second clue. <<WRITE_TEXT:prefix = carbon count|id=text-1>>The prefix tells you exactly how many carbon atoms are in the chain.

segments.raw_narration: Meth- means one carbon, eth- means two, prop- means three, and but- means four. So prop- tells me this molecule has exactly three carbon atoms.

segments.raw_narration: Here's an example from the chapter. For the alkanes, the general formula is C n H two n plus two, where n is just a number that tells you how many carbon atoms are in the molecule. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Use the general formula CnH2n+2 to find the formulas of methane, ethane, and propane|id=ex-q-1>>
segments.text_with_markers: Here's an example from the chapter. For the alkanes, the general formula is C n H two n plus two, where n is just a number that tells you how many carbon atoms are in the molecule. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Use the general formula CnH2n+2 to find the formulas of methane, ethane, and propane|id=ex-q-1>>

segments.raw_narration: Let's start with methane. For methane, n is one. So we put one in for n, and two times one plus two gives four hydrogens. That's C one H four, which we write as CH four. <<WRITE_STEP:Methane: n = 1, so C1H(2x1+2) = CH4|id=ex-step-1-1>>

segments.raw_narration: Next, ethane. For ethane, n is two. Two carbons, and two times two plus two gives six hydrogens. So that's C two H six. <<WRITE_STEP:Ethane: n = 2, so C2H(2x2+2) = C2H6|id=ex-step-1-2>>
segments.text_with_markers: Next, ethane. For ethane, n is two. Two carbons, and two times two plus two gives six hydrogens. So that's C two H six. <<WRITE_STEP:Ethane: n = 2, so C2H(2x2+2) = C2H6|id=ex-step-1-2>>

segments.raw_narration: And finally propane. For propane, n is three. Three carbons, and two times three plus two gives eight hydrogens. So that's C three H eight. <<WRITE_STEP:Propane: n = 3, so C3H(2x3+2) = C3H8|id=ex-step-1-3>>
segments.text_with_markers: And finally propane. For propane, n is three. Three carbons, and two times three plus two gives eight hydrogens. So that's C three H eight. <<WRITE_STEP:Propane: n = 3, so C3H(2x3+2) = C3H8|id=ex-step-1-3>>

segments.raw_narration: And there are our answers: methane is CH four, ethane is C two H six, and propane is C three H eight, all built straight from the general formula C n H two n plus two. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Methane CH4, Ethane C2H6, Propane C3H8|id=ex-ans-1>>

lesson_narrations.full_text_with_markers: There are more than ten million known organic compounds — and yet you will never have to memorize a single one of their names, because every name is secretly a code. Here is the trick that chemists worked out: instead of inventing a random name for each compound, they built the name out of two clues stuck together. <<FOCUS:full-name>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:organic_chemistry:17_4:name_decoder>> <<SECTION:The hidden code|id=sec-1>>Look at this name on the board — propanol. It looks like one word, but it is really two pieces of information glued together. <<FOCUS:suffix-part>> The ending of the name — the very last part — tells you which family the compound belongs to. <<POINT:suffix-part>> <<PAUSE:short>> If a name ends in -ane it is an alkane, if it ends in -ene it is an alkene, if it ends in -ol it is an alcohol, and if it ends in -oic acid it is a carboxylic acid. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:family-tag>> So this ending, -ol, immediately tells me: this compound is a member of the alcohol family. I did not have to look anything up. Now, the family alone is not enough — alcohols come in many sizes. So what tells me how big this particular molecule is? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:prefix-part>> The beginning of the name carries that second clue. <<WRITE_TEXT:prefix = carbon count|id=text-1>>The prefix tells you exactly how many carbon atoms are in the chain. <<POINT:prefix-part>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:carbon-chain>> Meth- means one carbon, eth- means two, prop- means three, and but- means four. So prop- tells me this molecule has exactly three carbon atoms. <<TRACE:carbon-chain>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:full-name>> <<WRITE_KEY:Name = (how many carbons) + (which family)|id=key-1>>Put the two clues together and the name decodes itself: prop plus ol means a three-carbon molecule in the alcohol family. Here's an example from the chapter. For the alkanes, the general formula is C n H two n plus two, where n is just a number that tells you how many carbon atoms are in the molecule. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Use the general formula CnH2n+2 to find the formulas of methane, ethane, and propane|id=ex-q-1>> Let's start with methane. For methane, n is one. So we put one in for n, and two times one plus two gives four hydrogens. That's C one H four, which we write as CH four. <<WRITE_STEP:Methane: n = 1, so C1H(2x1+2) = CH4|id=ex-step-1-1>> Next, ethane. For ethane, n is two. Three carbons, and two times three plus two gives eight hydrogens. Petroleum: a fossil fuel    
The fossil fuels 
The fossil fuels are petroleum (or crude oil), coal, and natural gas. 
They are called fossil fuels because they are the remains of plants and 
animals that lived millions of years ago. 
What is in petroleum?
Petroleum is a smelly mixture of hundreds of different compounds. 
They are organic compounds, which means they contain carbon, and 
usually hydrogen. 
In fact most are hydrocarbons – they contain only carbon and hydrogen. 
These drawings show molecules of three different hydrocarbons:

This is a molecule of pentane, 
C5H12. It has a straight chain of 
5 carbon atoms.
This is a molecule of cyclohexane, 
C6H12. Here a chain of 6 carbon 
atoms form a ring.
Petroleum formed from the 
remains of dead organisms that 
fell to the ocean floor, and were 
buried under thick sediment. High 
pressures slowly converted them to 
petroleum, over millions of years. 
Natural gas is mainly methane.  
It is often found with petroleum.  
It is formed in the same way.  
But high temperatures and high 
pressures caused the compounds 
to break down to gas.
Coal is the remains of lush 
vegetation that grew in ancient 
swamps. The dead vegetation was 
buried under thick sediment. 
Pressure and heat slowly converted 
it to coal, over millions of years.
This is a molecule of 3-methyl 
pentane, C6H14. Here 6 carbon 
atoms form a branched chain.
A formula drawn out in this way is called a structural formula.
Notice how the carbon atoms are bonded to each other, to make the spine  
of each molecule. The hydrogen atoms are bonded to the carbon atoms. 
In petroleum you will find hydrocarbon molecules of different shapes and 
sizes, with different numbers of carbon atoms, from 1 to over 70.

245
O r g a n i c  c h e m i s t r y
How we use petroleum
Over 13 billion litres of petroleum are used around the world every day.
Around half the petroleum pumped 
from oil wells is used for transport. 
It provides the fuel for cars, trucks, 
planes, and ships. You won’t get far 
without it!
Most of the rest is burned for heat, 
in factories, homes, and power 
stations, as above. In a power 
station, the heat is used to turn 
water to steam, to drive turbines.
A small % is used as the starting 
chemicals to make many other 
things: plastics, shampoo, paint, 
thread, fabric, detergents, 
makeup, medical drugs, and more.
 A platform for pumping petroleum from under the ocean.
Many of the things you use every day 
were probably made from petroleum. 
Toothbrush, comb, and shampoo just 
for a start!
A non-renewable resource
Petroleum is still forming, very slowly, 
under the oceans. But we are using it up 
much faster than it can form, which 
means it will run out one day.
So petroleum is called a non-renewable 
resource. 
It is hard to tell when it will run out. 
At the present rate of use, some experts 
say the world’s reserves will last about  
40 more years. What will we do then?

1	 The other name for petroleum is … ?
2	 Why is petroleum called a fossil fuel?
3	 What is a hydrocarbon?
4	 What is petroleum made of?
5	 Explain why petroleum is such a valuable resource.
6	 Petroleum is called a non-renewable resource. Why?

runs out?
topics.our_understanding:
Let's start with something you've probably heard about but maybe never thought deeply about: petroleum, also called crude oil. Petroleum is one of three fossil fuels, alongside coal and natural gas. We call them fossil fuels because they're the remains of plants and animals that lived millions of years ago. Think about that for a moment. The fuel in a car today started as living things in ancient oceans and swamps. When those organisms died, they fell to the ocean floor and got buried under thick layers of sediment. Over millions of years, enormous pressure slowly turned them into petroleum. Coal formed in a similar way, from lush vegetation in ancient swamps, squeezed and heated underground. Natural gas, which is mainly methane, formed when high temperatures and pressures broke compounds down into gas.

Now, what's actually inside petroleum? It's a smelly mixture of hundreds of different compounds. These are organic compounds, which means they contain carbon, and usually hydrogen too. Most of them are hydrocarbons, meaning they contain only carbon and hydrogen, nothing else. We can draw these molecules using what's called a structural formula, where you see exactly how the atoms are bonded. Notice that carbon atoms link to each other to form the spine of the molecule, and hydrogen atoms attach to those carbons. The shapes vary a lot. Some are straight chains, like pentane with five carbon atoms. Some form rings, like cyclohexane with six carbons in a circle. And some are branched, like three-methyl pentane. In petroleum you'll find molecules with anywhere from one carbon atom to over seventy.

Why does this matter to you? Because we use a staggering amount of it. Over thirteen billion liters of petroleum are used around the world every single day. About half goes to transport, fueling cars, trucks, planes, and ships. Most of the rest is burned for heat in factories, homes, and power stations, where heat turns water into steam to drive turbines. A small percentage becomes the raw material for plastics, shampoo, paint, fabric, makeup, and even medical drugs. Your toothbrush and comb probably came from petroleum.

Here's the catch. Petroleum is still forming, but incredibly slowly, while we use it up far faster than it can replace itself. That makes it a non-renewable resource, meaning it will run out one day. Some experts say the world's reserves might last only about forty more years at our current rate. So a big question for your generation is: what will we use when it's gone?

Then, over millions of years, enormous pressure and heat slowly squeezed and cooked those buried remains into something new entirely. <<PAUSE:short>> That something is petroleum, also called crude oil — and along with coal and natural gas, it is what we call a fossil fuel, because it really is made from ancient fossils. <<PAUSE:short>> But here is the strange part: if you could smell a drop of crude oil, you would be smelling not one substance, but hundreds of different compounds all mixed together. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:carbon-chain>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:organic_chemistry:17_1:hydrocarbon_skeletons>> <<SECTION:Hydrocarbons|id=sec-2>>So what are all these compounds made of? Almost all of them are built from just two kinds of atom — carbon and hydrogen — and we call those molecules hydrocarbons. <<PAUSE:short>> Watch this chain take shape. Each grey atom here is carbon, the backbone of the whole molecule. <<TRACE:carbon-chain>> <<POINT:carbon-chain>> <<WRITE_TEXT:C = carbon, H = hydrogen|id=text-1>>This carbon, marked C, links to its neighbours, and every spare arm grabs a hydrogen atom, marked H. Carbon and hydrogen — that is the whole recipe. <<POINT:carbon-atom-label>> <<POINT:carbon-atom-label>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:carbon-ring>> Now, why hundreds of different compounds? Because carbon is a master builder — the same atoms can connect in a straight chain, or curl right around into a ring. <<TRACE:carbon-ring>> Short chains, long chains, rings, branches — each different shape is a different compound, which is exactly why crude oil is such a rich mixture. <<POINT:hydrogen-atom-label>> <<FOCUS:carbon-chain>> <<WRITE_KEY:Petroleum = a mixture of hydrocarbons (carbon + hydrogen)|id=key-1>>So remember this: petroleum is not one chemical, it is a mixture of hydrocarbons, molecules made only from carbon and hydrogen. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> And every time you fill a tank, you are burning carbon chains that took an ocean, a graveyard of ancient life, and millions of years of pressure to build.

Refining petroleum
What does refining mean?
Petroleum contains hundreds of different hydrocarbons. But a big  
mixture like this is not very useful. 
So the first step is to separate the compounds into groups with molecules 
of a similar size. This is called refining the petroleum. It is carried out by 
fractional distillation.
Refining petroleum in the lab
The apparatus on the right can be used to refine petroleum in the lab. 
1	 As you heat the petroleum, the compounds start to evaporate.  
The ones with smaller lighter molecules go first, since it takes less 
energy to free these from the liquid.
2	 As the hot vapours rise, so does the thermometer reading.  
The vapours condense in the cool test-tube.
3	 When the thermometer reading reaches 100 °C, replace the first 
test-tube with an empty one. The liquid in the first test-tube is  
your first fraction from the distillation.
4	 Collect three further fractions in the same way, replacing the  
test-tube at 150 °C, 200 °C, and 300 °C. 
Comparing the fractions
Now compare the fractions – how runny they are, how easily they burn, 
and so on. You can burn samples on a watch glass, like this:

topics.our_understanding:
Imagine you've just pumped some crude oil, also called petroleum, out of the ground. If you looked at it closely, you'd find it's not one single substance at all. It's a giant mixture of hundreds of different hydrocarbons, which are compounds made of hydrogen and carbon. A big jumbled mixture like that isn't very useful, so the first job is to sort it out. We separate the compounds into groups whose molecules are all roughly the same size. This sorting process is called refining, and the method we use is called fractional distillation.

Here's the clever idea behind it. Different molecules boil off at different temperatures. Small, light molecules need only a little energy to escape the liquid, so they evaporate first at low temperatures. Bigger, heavier molecules hang on tight and only boil off when things get really hot. So if you slowly heat petroleum and collect the vapours as the temperature climbs, you naturally separate the mixture by molecule size. In the lab, you heat the petroleum, watch the thermometer, and swap test tubes at certain temperatures. Each batch you collect is called a fraction.

When you compare the fractions, a beautiful pattern appears. The first fraction, made of small molecules, is very runny, it evaporates easily, which we call volatile, and it catches fire and burns very easily. As you move to fractions with bigger molecules, the liquid gets thicker, or more viscous, less volatile, and harder to burn. The last one barely lights at all and needs a wick.

So remember this golden rule: the larger the molecules in a hydrocarbon, the higher its boiling point, the less volatile it is, the less easily it flows, and the less easily it burns. These trends decide what each fraction is good for.

In a real refinery, this happens in a tall tower that is very hot at the bottom, over four hundred degrees Celsius, and cool near the top. Petroleum is pumped in at the base, the compounds boil off, and the smallest molecules rise highest before condensing. From top to bottom you get refinery gas for cooking, gasoline for cars, naphtha for making chemicals and plastics, paraffin for aircraft, diesel oil, fuel oil, lubricating oil, and finally bitumen for road surfaces. Notice how a messy mixture becomes a whole shelf of useful products, just by sorting molecules by size.

topics.our_understanding: Let's talk about what happens to petroleum after it has been separated by fractional distillation. You might think that once we've split crude oil into its fractions, the job is done. But it isn't. Those fractions still need extra treatment before they're useful. First, they contain impurities, mostly sulfur compounds. If we left those in the fuel, they would burn and form harmful sulfur dioxide gas, so we remove them. Second, some fractions get split even further into single compounds. For instance, the gas fraction is separated into methane, ethane, propane, and butane, which is the gas we buy in canisters. And third, part of a fraction may be cracked. Cracking is the star of this section, so let's focus on it. Cracking simply means breaking big molecules down into smaller ones. Imagine you have long chains of carbon atoms. When you heat them strongly, often over a catalyst, the chains snap into shorter pieces. We call this a thermal decomposition, because heat causes a single substance to break apart. In the lab, you take a hydrocarbon oil, soak it into mineral wool, heat it, and pass the vapor over a hot aluminium oxide catalyst. The starting material is a thick, smelly-free liquid that's hard to burn, which tells you it has large molecules with long carbon chains. But the product is a colorless gas that smells sharp, burns easily, and reacts readily. That tells you it has small molecules with short chains. Nothing new was added, so the product must still be a hydrocarbon, just a smaller one. One safety point to remember, the instant you stop heating, lift the delivery tube out of the water, otherwise water gets sucked back into the hot test tube and could crack it. Now, why does cracking matter so much? Two big reasons. First, it lets you make the best use of petroleum. If you have too much naphtha and not enough gasoline, you can crack the naphtha into molecules the right size for petrol. Second, cracking always produces short-chain compounds that contain a carbon to carbon double bond. That double bond makes the molecules reactive, which is exactly what we want for making plastics and many other useful chemicals. So cracking turns leftover, less useful long molecules into valuable, reactive small ones.

So decane has been broken down into three smaller molecules. The propene and ethene molecules have carbon–carbon double bonds. These two compounds belong to the alkene family, and they are very reactive.

We call that an alkane, and it is exactly the smaller, lighter fuel we wanted. <<TRACE:small-alkane>> <<FOCUS:small-alkene>> But here is the catch. When the chain snapped, this other piece was left short of hydrogen. Two of its carbons grab each other extra tightly instead. <<TRACE:small-alkene>> <<FOCUS:double-bond>> <<WRITE_TEXT:alkene = has a C=C double bond|id=text-1>>That extra-tight grip is a double bond between two carbon atoms. A molecule with a carbon-to-carbon double bond is called an alkene. Why should anyone care about that double bond? It looks like a small detail on the picture. <<POINT:double-bond>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:double-bond>> <<WRITE_KEY:Cracking makes an alkane AND an alkene; the alkene builds plastics|id=key-2>>Because that double bond is hungry to react. It lets thousands of alkene molecules link up into long chains, and those long chains are plastics. No cracking, no plastic. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:small-alkane>> So one big useless molecule becomes two prizes at once: a useful small fuel, and a reactive alkene for making materials. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter. We take decane, with the formula C ten H twenty-two, which comes from the naphtha fraction. We heat it to five hundred and forty degrees Celsius with a catalyst, and it cracks into smaller molecules. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Crack decane (C10H22) from naphtha at 540 C with a catalyst|id=ex-q-1>> One large hydrocarbon breaks down into one smaller alkane plus one alkene, and every atom is conserved. <<WRITE_EQUATION:C_{10}H_{22} \rightarrow C_{8}H_{18} + C_{2}H_{4}|id=eq-1|boxed>> We start by writing the reactant. One molecule of decane, C ten H twenty-two, contains ten carbon atoms and twenty-two hydrogen atoms. <<WRITE_STEP:Reactant: C10H22 (10 carbons, 22 hydrogens)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now we break it into three smaller molecules. It gives pentane, C five H twelve, which is suitable for petrol, plus propene, C three H six, plus ethene, C two H four. <<WRITE_STEP:Products: C5H12 + C3H6 + C2H4|id=ex-step-1-2>> Let's check the atoms balance. On the product side the carbons are five plus three plus two, which makes ten carbons, matching the decane. The hydrogens are twelve plus six plus four, which makes twenty-two hydrogens, again matching. So ten carbons and twenty-two hydrogens split cleanly into three molecules. <<WRITE_STEP:Carbons: 5+3+2 = 10. Hydrogens: 12+6+4 = 22.|id=ex-step-1-3>> Notice that propene and ethene each contain a carbon-to-carbon double bond. They belong to the alkene family, and that double bond makes them very reactive. <<WRITE_STEP:Propene and ethene are alkenes with C=C double bonds, very reactive|id=ex-step-1-4>> And the answer is that decane has been broken down into three smaller molecules: pentane, suitable for petrol, plus the reactive alkenes propene and ethene. <<WRITE_ANSWER:C10H22 -> C5H12 + C3H6 + C2H4|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Ethane has very short molecules, but even it can be cracked. We take ethane and pass it with steam at greater than eight hundred degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Crack ethane using steam at over 800 degrees Celsius. What forms?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by breaking the ethane molecule apart under those harsh conditions. Cracking always pulls out a small reactive piece, leaving behind a molecule with a double bond. So ethane splits to give ethene plus hydrogen, that is, H two. <<WRITE_STEP:Ethane, with steam at greater than 800 degrees Celsius, gives ethene plus hydrogen (H2)|id=ex-step-1-1>> And the answer is ethene and hydrogen. Notice we get that reactive double-bonded product, ethene, and the hydrogen produced can be used to make ammonia. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Products: ethene + hydrogen (H2); the hydrogen can be used to make ammonia|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. After crude oil is fractionally distilled, some of the fractions are still mixtures, so they get split further into individual compounds. Take the gas fraction as our case. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What does the gas fraction separate into?|id=ex-q-1>> The gas fraction is separated into four individual compounds: methane, ethane, propane, and butane. <<WRITE_STEP:Gas fraction -> methane, ethane, propane, butane|id=ex-step-1-1>> And here's the everyday connection: butane is the one we buy in canisters. So the gas fraction yields methane, ethane, propane, and butane, with butane sold in canisters. <<WRITE_ANSWER:methane, ethane, propane, butane (butane sold in canisters)|id=ex-ans-1>> <<FOCUS:long-chain>> And because heat alone tore that strong molecule apart, chemists give cracking its proper name: thermal decomposition, breaking down using heat. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:small-alkene>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:C_{10}H_{22} \rightarrow C_{8}H_{18} + C_{2}H_{4}|id=eq-1>>In symbols, one large hydrocarbon arrow gives one smaller alkane plus one alkene. Count the atoms on each side and you will see nothing is lost, just rearranged.

topics.our_understanding: Let's make sense of organic chemistry, which can feel overwhelming at first because there are literally millions of organic compounds. The good news is that chemists organized everything in a clever, logical way, so once you learn the system you can understand a huge number of compounds without memorizing each one. Here's the big idea: organic compounds are sorted into families, and the name of a compound tells you two things at once. It tells you which family it belongs to, and it tells you how many carbon atoms are in it. Think of it like a code hidden inside the name. The ending of the name reveals the family. If a name ends in -ane, it's an alkane. If it ends in -ene, it's an alkene. If it ends in -ol, it's an alcohol. And if it ends in -oic acid, it's a carboxylic acid. The beginning of the name tells you the number of carbon atoms. Meth- means one carbon, eth- means two, prop- means three, but- means four, pent- means five, and hex- means six. So if I say propanol, you can decode it instantly: prop- means three carbons, and -ol means it's an alcohol. The simplest family is the alkanes, and the simplest alkane is methane, which is the main gas burning on a cooker hob. The alkanes contain only carbon and hydrogen, so we call them hydrocarbons, and all their carbon-to-carbon bonds are single bonds. Now here's a key idea called a functional group. A functional group is the part of a molecule that mostly decides how it will react. For example, all alkenes react in similar ways because they all share the same functional group, a carbon-to-carbon double bond. The alcohols share an O-H group, and the carboxylic acids share a C-O-O-H group. Finally, each family forms what we call a homologous series. In a homologous series, all the compounds fit the same general formula. For the alkanes, that formula is C-n-H-two-n-plus-two, where n is the number of carbon atoms. The chain length grows by one carbon each time, and as the chain gets longer, the properties change gradually. Notice that boiling points rise, the liquids flow less easily, and the compounds burn less easily. Once you see these patterns, organic chemistry stops being a list to memorize and becomes a system you can predict.

topics.standalone_narration_text: There are more than ten million known organic compounds — and yet you will never have to memorize a single one of their names, because every name is secretly a code. Here is the trick that chemists worked out: instead of inventing a random name for each compound, they built the name out of two clues stuck together. <<FOCUS:full-name>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:organic_chemistry:17_4:name_decoder>> <<SECTION:The hidden code|id=sec-1>>Look at this name on the board — propanol. It looks like one word, but it is really two pieces of information glued together. <<FOCUS:suffix-part>> The ending of the name — the very last part — tells you which family the compound belongs to. <<POINT:suffix-part>> <<PAUSE:short>> If a name ends in -ane it is an alkane, if it ends in -ene it is an alkene, if it ends in -ol it is an alcohol, and if it ends in -oic acid it is a carboxylic acid. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:family-tag>> So this ending, -ol, immediately tells me: this compound is a member of the alcohol family. I did not have to look anything up. Now, the family alone is not enough — alcohols come in many sizes. So what tells me how big this particular molecule is? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:prefix-part>> The beginning of the name carries that second clue. <<WRITE_TEXT:prefix = carbon count|id=text-1>>The prefix tells you exactly how many carbon atoms are in the chain. <<POINT:prefix-part>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:carbon-chain>> Meth- means one carbon, eth- means two, prop- means three, and but- means four. So prop- tells me this molecule has exactly three carbon atoms. <<TRACE:carbon-chain>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:full-name>> <<WRITE_KEY:Name = (how many carbons) + (which family)|id=key-1>>Put the two clues together and the name decodes itself: prop plus ol means a three-carbon molecule in the alcohol family. Here's an example from the chapter. For the alkanes, the general formula is C n H two n plus two, where n is just a number that tells you how many carbon atoms are in the molecule. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Use the general formula CnH2n+2 to find the formulas of methane, ethane, and propane|id=ex-q-1>> Let's start with methane. For methane, n is one. So we put one in for n, and two times one plus two gives four hydrogens. That's C one H four, which we write as CH four. <<WRITE_STEP:Methane: n = 1, so C1H(2x1+2) = CH4|id=ex-step-1-1>> Next, ethane. For ethane, n is two. Two carbons, and two times two plus two gives six hydrogens. So that's C two H six. <<WRITE_STEP:Ethane: n = 2, so C2H(2x2+2) = C2H6|id=ex-step-1-2>> And finally propane. For propane, n is three. Three carbons, and two times three plus two gives eight hydrogens. So that's C three H eight. <<WRITE_STEP:Propane: n = 3, so C3H(2x3+2) = C3H8|id=ex-step-1-3>> And there are our answers: methane is CH four, ethane is C two H six, and propane is C three H eight, all built straight from the general formula C n H two n plus two. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Methane CH4, Ethane C2H6, Propane C3H8|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Let's look at the first four members of the alkane family and watch what happens to their boiling points. Methane has one carbon atom, ethane has two carbon atoms, propane has three carbon atoms, and butane has four carbon atoms. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How does boiling point change from methane to butane?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by listing each one with its boiling point. Methane, with just one carbon, has the lowest boiling point at about minus one hundred sixty-four degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Methane (1 C): about -164 degrees C|id=ex-step-1-1>> Ethane, with two carbons, boils a little higher. <<WRITE_STEP:Ethane (2 C): higher than methane|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now we keep going up the chain. Propane, with three carbons, boils at about minus forty-two degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Propane (3 C): about -42 degrees C|id=ex-step-1-3>> And butane, with four carbons, boils at about minus zero point five degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Butane (4 C): about -0.5 degrees C|id=ex-step-1-4>> Look at the pattern: each time we add a carbon, the boiling point climbs. So the answer is clear, the boiling point increases as the chain length increases. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Boiling point increases as chain length increases (methane < ethane < propane < butane)|id=ex-ans-1>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> And the simplest family of all, the alkanes, shows the pattern beautifully: methane has one carbon, ethane two, propane three, butane four — and as the chains get longer, the boiling points climb steadily upward. So once you know the endings and the beginnings, you have not learned one compound — you have learned how to read millions of them at a glance.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's get to know the alkanes, which are the simplest family of organic compounds. The word hydrocarbon tells you exactly what they're made of: only carbon and hydrogen, nothing else. What makes alkanes special is that all of their carbon-to-carbon bonds are single bonds. Because every bond is a single bond, with no spare bonds left over, we call the alkanes saturated. Picture ethane: two carbon atoms joined by one shared pair of electrons, which is a single bond, and each carbon is also holding onto hydrogen atoms. That sharing of one pair is what a single bond means.

The alkanes form what we call a homologous series, which is a family where each member differs from the next by one carbon and two hydrogens. Their general formula is C-n-H-two-n-plus-two, meaning if you know the number of carbons, you can work out the hydrogens. The first four are methane, ethane, propane, and butane, and they're all gases at room temperature. The next twelve are liquids, and the rest are solids. Notice the pattern in boiling points: the longer the carbon chain, the higher the boiling point. That's because longer molecules attract each other more strongly, so you need more energy to pull them apart.

Where do we find them? In petroleum and natural gas. Natural gas is mostly methane. Alkanes are generally quite unreactive, but they do one very important thing well: they burn. With plenty of oxygen, they form carbon dioxide and water vapour and release lots of heat, which is why we use them as fuels. But here's a warning. If there isn't enough oxygen, they undergo incomplete combustion and make carbon monoxide, which is poisonous and gives out less heat.

Alkanes also react with chlorine, but only in sunlight. This is a substitution reaction, because a chlorine atom takes the place of a hydrogen atom one at a time. It's also called photochemical, meaning light energy is needed to start it by breaking the bonds in chlorine.

Finally, meet isomers: compounds with the same formula but different structures. Butane and two-methylpropane both have the formula C-four-H-ten, but one chain is straight and the other is branched. The more carbons, the more isomers possible. And branched isomers have lower boiling points, because the branches keep molecules from getting close, so the attraction between them is weaker.

Here is ethane, and you can see its skeleton is just two carbon atoms, with hydrogen atoms hanging off the outside, nothing else in the whole molecule. <<POINT:hydrogens>> <<POINT:hydrogens>> <<FOCUS:cc-bond>> Now look right at the middle, at the link joining the two carbons together. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> That link is one shared pair of electrons, and one shared pair is exactly what we mean by a single bond. <<TRACE:cc-bond>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:cc-bond>> <<WRITE_KEY:Every C-C bond is single, so alkanes are saturated|id=key-1>>And this is the rule for the whole family: every carbon-to-carbon bond is a single bond, with no spare bonds left over, which is why we call the alkanes saturated. <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:A family with a pattern|id=sec-2>>The alkanes aren't just one molecule though, they're a whole series, and the series follows a beautifully simple pattern. Start with methane, one carbon. Add a carbon and two hydrogens and you get ethane. Add another carbon and two more hydrogens and you get propane. So if I just told you a molecule has ten carbons, could you tell me exactly how many hydrogens it must have, without ever seeing it? <<PAUSE:long>> Because each member differs from the next by one carbon and two hydrogens, the number of hydrogens is always two times the number of carbons, plus two more. <<WRITE_EQUATION:C_nH_{2n+2}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Each step: +1 carbon, +2 hydrogens|id=key-2>>Yes, you can, because each member differs from the next by one carbon and two hydrogens, and that locks in the formula carbon-n hydrogen two-n-plus-two. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter. When methane burns in a good supply of oxygen, it undergoes complete combustion. We start with one molecule of methane, that's C H four, reacting with two molecules of oxygen, two O two. The reaction needs that good supply of oxygen to burn cleanly. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What is the complete combustion of methane?|id=ex-q-1>> Now we write the reactants on the left. One methane molecule plus two oxygen molecules. <<WRITE_STEP:Reactants: one C H four plus two O two|id=ex-step-1-1>><<WRITE_EQUATION:CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow|id=ex-eq-1>> These react together to form the products. One molecule of methane gives one carbon dioxide, that's one C O two, plus two molecules of water, two H two O, and it releases plenty of heat energy. So the answer is: C H four plus two O two gives one C O two plus two H two O plus heat energy. <<WRITE_ANSWER:CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O + heat energy|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. When there isn't enough oxygen, alkanes undergo incomplete combustion, and instead of carbon dioxide they produce poisonous carbon monoxide. Let's balance the equation for methane burning in too little oxygen. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Write the incomplete combustion of methane in insufficient oxygen|id=ex-q-1>> We start on the left side with two molecules of methane reacting with three molecules of oxygen. Because there isn't enough oxygen, the carbon can't fully oxidise. <<WRITE_STEP:2 CH4 + 3 O2 -> ?|id=ex-step-1-1>> Working out the products: the carbon ends up as carbon monoxide, so we get two molecules of carbon monoxide, and the hydrogen forms four molecules of water. And critically, this reaction releases less heat energy than complete combustion, all because there is not enough oxygen. <<WRITE_STEP:Products: 2 CO + 4 H2O + less heat|id=ex-step-1-2>> And the answer is the balanced equation: two methane plus three oxygen gives two carbon monoxide plus four water, releasing less heat energy. <<WRITE_ANSWER:2 CH4 (g) + 3 O2 (g) -> 2 CO (g) + 4 H2O (l) + less heat energy|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Methane reacts with chlorine, that's C-l-two, but only in sunlight. The light is essential because it breaks the chlorine bonds, so this is a photochemical reaction. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What happens when methane reacts with chlorine in sunlight?|id=ex-q-1>> We start with the first reaction. In sunlight, methane plus chlorine produces chloromethane, C-H-three-C-l, plus hydrogen chloride, H-C-l. topics.our_understanding:
Let's meet a new family of carbon compounds called the alkenes. Like the alkanes you may have already studied, the alkenes are hydrocarbons, which simply means they're made of only two elements, carbon and hydrogen. And like the alkanes, they form what we call a homologous series, which is just a fancy way of saying a family where each member follows the same pattern and differs from the next by a fixed building block. For the alkenes, that pattern is captured in their general formula, where the number of hydrogen atoms is always exactly twice the number of carbon atoms. So if you tell me how many carbons there are, I can tell you the hydrogens instantly.

Now here's the most important thing about this family, the feature that makes them special. Every alkene contains a carbon-to-carbon double bond. Think of it as two carbon atoms holding hands not with one bond but with two. This double bond is what we call the functional group, and the functional group is the active part of the molecule that controls how it reacts. So when you understand the double bond, you understand most of alkene chemistry.

Because they have this double bond, alkenes are described as unsaturated. Compare that to the alkanes, which only have single carbon-to-carbon bonds, so we call them saturated. A nice way to remember it is that a saturated molecule is full up, every bond used on holding single neighbours, while an unsaturated molecule has that extra bonding tucked into the double bond.

Let's look at the first three members of the family. The smallest is ethene, with two carbon atoms and four hydrogen atoms. Next comes propene, with three carbons and six hydrogens. Then but-one-ene, with four carbons and eight hydrogens. Notice the pattern holding true each time, the hydrogens are always double the carbons. Notice too how the boiling points climb as the molecules get bigger and heavier, just as you'd expect, since larger molecules attract each other more strongly and need more energy to pull apart into a gas. So as you go down this family, the trend is steady and predictable, and that predictability is exactly why chemists love thinking in terms of homologous series.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's meet a whole family of organic compounds called the alcohols. What makes something an alcohol? It's the presence of a special group of atoms called the O-H group, that's an oxygen joined to a hydrogen. Whenever you see that group hanging off a carbon chain, you're looking at an alcohol. The first four members are methanol, ethanol, propan-one-ol, and butan-one-ol. They form what we call a homologous series, which is just a fancy way of saying they're a family that follows a regular pattern. Their general formula is C-n-H-two-n-plus-one-O-H, meaning that as you add carbon atoms one at a time, the formula changes in a steady, predictable way. Notice that their boiling points climb as the chains get longer, from sixty-five degrees Celsius for methanol up to one hundred seventeen degrees for butanol. Because they all share that same O-H group, they all react in similar ways. And when a name has a one in it, like propan-one-ol, that tells you the O-H group sits on a carbon at the end of the chain.

The star of this section is ethanol. It's the alcohol in alcoholic drinks, it's a great solvent that dissolves things water can't, and it evaporates easily, which we call being volatile. That's why it's used in glues, inks, perfumes, and aftershave.

There are two ways to make ethanol. The first is fermentation, the biological way, where yeast turns glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide without air. The enzymes in the living yeast act as catalysts, and the reaction gives out heat, so it's exothermic. The yeast eventually stops when there's too much ethanol or it gets too warm, and then the ethanol is separated by fractional distillation. The second way is hydration of ethene, the chemical way, where water is added to ethene using high pressure, a temperature of about five hundred seventy degrees Celsius, and a phosphoric acid catalyst.

Ethanol also works as a fuel. It burns well in oxygen to make carbon dioxide and water, giving plenty of heat. It's attractive because it can be made cheaply from waste plant material, and it has less impact on carbon dioxide levels than fossil fuels. Here's the clever part: when ethanol burns it does release carbon dioxide, but the plants grown to make more ethanol soak that carbon dioxide back up. Fossil fuels, by contrast, release carbon that was locked away millions of years ago. The drawback, though, is that growing crops for fuel uses land we could use for food, which can raise food prices and hurt poor people most.

So the answer: glucose ferments to give two molecules of ethanol plus two molecules of carbon dioxide plus energy, then the ethanol is recovered by fractional distillation. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Fermentation: C6H12O6 -> 2 C2H5OH + 2 CO2 + energy; ethanol separated by fractional distillation|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We want to make ethanol the chemical way, by the hydration of ethene. Hydration means water is added on, so this is an addition reaction where ethene, C two H four, reacts with water, H two O. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: How is ethanol made by hydration of ethene?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by writing the reaction. Ethene gas plus water vapour gives ethanol, a liquid. This is carried out at a temperature of five hundred and seventy degrees Celsius and a pressure of sixty to seventy atmospheres, using a catalyst of phosphoric acid. <<WRITE_STEP:C2H4 (g) + H2O (g) -> C2H5OH (l)|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:Conditions: 570 degrees C, 60-70 atm, phosphoric acid catalyst|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now notice the reaction is reversible and exothermic. In theory, high pressure and a low temperature would give the best yield. But in practice a high temperature of five hundred and seventy degrees Celsius is used to give a good rate of reaction, and the phosphoric acid catalyst speeds it up further. So the answer is: ethanol is made by adding water to ethene at five hundred and seventy degrees Celsius and sixty to seventy atmospheres over a phosphoric acid catalyst, in a reversible, exothermic addition reaction. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Ethanol made by hydration of ethene: C2H4 + H2O -> C2H5OH, at 570 C, 60-70 atm, phosphoric acid catalyst (reversible, exothermic)|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We take one molecule of liquid ethanol, C two H five O H, and burn it in oxygen. The question is: what does it produce, and why does that make it a good fuel? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Combustion of ethanol in oxygen|id=ex-q-1>> We start by writing the reactants. One molecule of ethanol reacts with three molecules of oxygen, O two. <<WRITE_STEP:C2H5OH (l) + 3 O2 (g) -> ...|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now we balance the products. The carbons go into carbon dioxide, giving two molecules of carbon dioxide, C O two, and the hydrogens go into water, giving three molecules of liquid water, H two O. Crucially, the reaction also releases heat. <<WRITE_STEP:... -> 2 CO2 (g) + 3 H2O (l) + heat|id=ex-step-1-2>> And so the answer is: one molecule of ethanol plus three molecules of oxygen gives two molecules of carbon dioxide, three molecules of water, and heat. That released heat is exactly why ethanol works as a fuel. <<WRITE_ANSWER:C2H5OH (l) + 3 O2 (g) -> 2 CO2 (g) + 3 H2O (l) + heat|id=ex-ans-1>> This is the real power of a homologous series: meet one member and understand its O-H group, and you can predict how every cousin in the family behaves. <<WRITE_TEXT:same O-H group = similar reactions|id=text-2>> <<POINT:oh-group>> <<FOCUS:oh-group>> So remember the one idea that unlocks all of organic chemistry's families: find the functional group — for alcohols that is the O-H — and you have found what the whole family has in common. <<PAUSE:short>>

topics.our_understanding: In this section we meet a new family of organic compounds called the carboxylic acids. The simplest four are methanoic acid, ethanoic acid, propanoic acid, and butanoic acid, holding one, two, three, and four carbon atoms in that order. Just like the other families you've seen, these form a homologous series, which means each member differs from the next by one carbon atom and they all share a general formula. For the carboxylic acids that general formula is C-n-H-two-n-O-two. Notice that as the molecules get bigger, their boiling points climb steadily, from about one hundred one degrees Celsius for methanoic acid up to one hundred sixty four degrees for butanoic acid. They all share the same special functional group, written as C-O-O-H, which we call the carboxyl group. That group is what gives the whole family its acidic character, so once you understand ethanoic acid, you understand them all. Ethanoic acid is the famous one — it's the main ingredient in vinegar. There are two ways to make it, and both involve oxidising ethanol. The biological way is acid fermentation, where bacteria left in air slowly oxidise ethanol into ethanoic acid; this is how vinegar is made from things like apples, rice, and honey. The chemical way is faster: you warm ethanol with a powerful oxidising agent, potassium manganate seven, in acid, and watch the purple color fade to colorless as the manganate is reduced. Potassium dichromate six works too, turning orange to green. Now, ethanoic acid behaves like a typical acid. It turns litmus red, it contains hydrogen ions, and it reacts with metals, bases, and carbonates to form salts. But here's a key idea: only some of its molecules split apart, or dissociate, in water, so it's called a weak acid. When it reacts with sodium hydroxide, it makes the salt sodium ethanoate plus water. Finally, ethanoic acid reacts with alcohols to make esters. When ethanoic acid meets propanol with concentrated sulfuric acid as a catalyst, you get propyl ethanoate plus water. Because two molecules join and a small water molecule is lost, we call this a condensation reaction, and it's reversible. Esters smell wonderful — propyl ethanoate smells of pears — so they're used in shampoos, soaps, and food flavorings.

Propanoic acid has three carbon atoms and boils at one hundred and forty-one degrees Celsius, and butanoic acid has four carbon atoms and boils at one hundred and sixty-four degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_STEP:Propanoic acid, 3 carbons, boiling point 141 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<WRITE_STEP:Butanoic acid, 4 carbons, boiling point 164 degrees Celsius|id=ex-step-1-4>> So as the molecules get bigger, from one carbon up to four carbons, the boiling point climbs steadily, from one hundred and one degrees Celsius all the way up to one hundred and sixty-four degrees Celsius. The boiling points of the carboxylic acids rise as the molecules get bigger. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Boiling points rise with size: 101, 118, 141, 164 degrees Celsius for 1 to 4 carbons|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We oxidise ethanol much faster by warming it with a powerful oxidising agent, potassium manganate seven, in the presence of acid. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Oxidise ethanol to ethanoic acid using potassium manganate(VII) in acid — what is the colour change?|id=ex-q-1>> The manganate seven ions are themselves reduced to Mn two plus ions, and the acid provides the H plus ions for the reaction. <<WRITE_STEP:Acid provides H+ ions for the reaction|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:MnO_4^- + 8H^+ + 5e^- \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O|id=ex-eq-1>> So the colour change tells us it has worked: with potassium manganate seven the colour goes from purple to colourless. Alternative — potassium dichromate(VI): orange → green.|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Sodium ethanoate is the salt here, and like all salts it is an ionic compound, which confirms ethanoic acid behaves as a typical acid. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Products: sodium ethanoate (the salt, an ionic compound) + water|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Ethanoic acid reacts with propanol, using concentrated sulfuric acid as the catalyst. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Ethanoic acid + propanol, with conc. sulfuric acid — what forms?|id=ex-q-1>> When these two react, they join together and lose a small molecule of water — so this is called a condensation reaction. The products are propyl ethanoate and water. <<WRITE_STEP:ethanoic acid + propanol → propyl ethanoate + water|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:CH_3COOH + C_3H_7OH \xrightarrow{\text{conc. } H_2SO_4} CH_3COOC_3H_7 + H_2O|id=ex-eq-1>> And the answer: the product is propyl ethanoate, which is an ester — and it smells of pears. Notice the reaction is reversible, and the sulfuric acid acts as a catalyst. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Propyl ethanoate (an ester, smells of pears) + water; reversible, sulfuric acid catalyst|id=ex-ans-1>> <<FOCUS:boiling-trend>> And because the molecules get heavier as the chain grows, look how their boiling points climb steadily, from around one hundred one degrees Celsius for the smallest up to one hundred sixty four degrees for butanoic acid. <<TRACE:boiling-trend>> <<FOCUS:carboxyl-group>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> So the next time vinegar makes your eyes water, remember it is this one little carboxyl group doing the work, the same group hiding in every acid in the family. <<PAUSE:short>>

topics.our_understanding:
In this section we're getting to know the alkenes, a family of hydrocarbons that share one special feature: a carbon-to-carbon double bond. That double bond is the whole story here. Let me show you why it matters.

First, where do alkenes come from? We make them by cracking alkanes. For instance, if you take ethane and heat it with steam above eight hundred degrees Celsius, it breaks apart into ethene and hydrogen gas. So cracking takes a saturated molecule and produces an unsaturated one plus some leftover hydrogen.

Now, why are alkenes so much more reactive than alkanes? Because that double bond can break open and grab extra atoms. Picture the double bond as a doorway that's ready to swing open. When it opens, the molecule can add things on. Ethene can add hydrogen back on, with a catalyst and heat and pressure, to become ethane again. Ethene can also add water as steam to become ethanol, which is an alcohol. We call these addition reactions because the molecule is literally adding atoms onto itself. When an unsaturated alkene adds atoms across the double bond, it becomes a saturated compound.

There's a really useful addition reaction called polymerisation. Here, alkene molecules add onto each other, over and over, forming chains thousands of carbon atoms long. The small starting molecules are called monomers, and the giant chains are called polymers. When ethene does this, you get poly-ethene, or polythene, the plastic in bags and bottles.

We also have a simple test for unsaturation. Bromine water is an orange solution. If you shake it with something that has a carbon-to-carbon double bond, an addition reaction happens and the orange colour disappears. So fading orange means a double bond is present.

Finally, alkenes can form isomers. Three different molecules can all share the formula C four H eight, yet have different structures because the chain branches differently or the double bond sits in a different spot. Their names, like but-one-ene and but-two-ene, use numbers to tell you exactly where that double bond lives.

topics.standalone_narration_text: <<FOCUS:ethene-double-bond>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:chemistry:organic_chemistry:26_5:ethene_vs_ethane>> Here are two molecules. One sits in a jar for years doing nothing; the other grabs onto almost anything you throw at it. Same two ingredients, carbon and hydrogen, so what makes the difference? <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:ethene-double-bond>> Look right at the centre of this molecule. The two carbon atoms are joined not by one line, but by two. That is a double bond, and it is the entire story of the alkenes. <<POINT:ethene-double-bond>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:ethene-hydrogens>> <<SECTION:Counting the hydrogens|id=sec-1>>Now let us count. This molecule is ethene. Each carbon holds two hydrogen atoms, so four hydrogens in total around two carbons. <<FOCUS:ethane-extra-hydrogens>> Beside it is ethane, the lazy one. Its carbons are joined by a single bond, and look, it has room for two extra hydrogen atoms that ethene simply does not have. <<POINT:ethane-extra-hydrogens>> So why does an alkene always have exactly twice as many hydrogens as carbons, the pattern we write as C-n-H-2-n? <<POINT:ethene-double-bond>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:ethene-double-bond>> Because making that second bond between the carbons uses up a pair of hands that would otherwise hold hydrogens. The double bond literally costs the molecule one pair of hydrogen atoms. <<PAUSE:short>> For an alkene with any number of carbons, you always get exactly twice as many hydrogen atoms as carbon atoms. <<WRITE_EQUATION:C_nH_{2n}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:ethene-double-bond>> <<WRITE_KEY:Every alkene fits C-n-H-2-n because the double bond costs one pair of hydrogens|id=key-1>>That is why every member of the family, two carbons, three carbons, ten carbons, always lands on twice as many hydrogens as carbons. The formula is C-n-H-2-n, and now you can see exactly where it comes from. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:ethene-double-bond>> <<SECTION:Why alkenes are so reactive|id=sec-2>>Now here is the beautiful part. Picture that double bond as a doorway. One of the two bonds can swing open, leaving each carbon with a free hand ready to grab a new atom. <<TRACE:ethene-double-bond>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:ethene-carbon-left>> <<WRITE_TEXT:double bond opens, atoms add on|id=text-1>>When that doorway opens and new atoms attach, we call it an addition reaction. Ethene can add hydrogen back on to become ethane, or add water to become ethanol. <<POINT:ethene-carbon-left>> Here's an example from the chapter. We make alkenes from alkanes by a process called cracking. In this case, our starting material is ethane, and we pass it together with steam over a catalyst at a temperature of over eight hundred degrees Celsius. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Crack ethane with steam at over 800 C — what forms?|id=ex-q-1>> When we crack ethane under these conditions, the molecule breaks apart. The carbon chain rearranges to form a carbon-to-carbon double bond, giving us ethene, and at the same time a molecule of hydrogen is released. <<WRITE_STEP:ethane + steam, over 800 C → cracking|id=ex-step-1-1>> So the products are ethene and hydrogen. Ethane, with steam at over eight hundred degrees Celsius, gives ethene plus hydrogen. <<WRITE_ANSWER:ethane → ethene + hydrogen|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Ethene, which is a gas, reacts with hydrogen gas in an addition reaction. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What does ethene form when it reacts with hydrogen?|id=ex-q-1>> For this reaction to happen, we need a catalyst, along with heat and pressure. Under those conditions, the hydrogen adds across the double bond of ethene. <<WRITE_STEP:Ethene (gas) + hydrogen gas, with a catalyst, heat and pressure|id=ex-step-1-1>> The product is ethane gas, a saturated molecule. So the answer is: ethene plus hydrogen gives ethane gas. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Ethene + H2 -> ethane (gas)|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Ethene, which is a gas, reacts with water in the form of steam. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What does ethene form when it adds water across its double bond?|id=ex-q-1>> For this reaction to happen, we need a catalyst, along with heat and pressure. Under those conditions, ethene adds water across its double bond. <<WRITE_STEP:Ethene (gas) plus water as steam, with a catalyst, heat and pressure|id=ex-step-1>> And the product is ethanol, a liquid alcohol. <<WRITE_ANSWER:The product is ethanol, a liquid alcohol|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Take ethene as our starting molecule, the monomer, and let it undergo polymerisation. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Many ethene monomers join by polymerisation — what forms?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by joining many ethene molecules together. Each ethene monomer links to the next, opening its double bond so the units chain end to end. <<WRITE_STEP:Step 1: Many ethene monomers (the monomer) join by polymerisation.|id=ex-step-1-1>> And the answer is that the product is poly of ethene, also called polythene, and this chain can be many thousands of carbon atoms long. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Product = poly(ethene) / polythene — chains many thousands of carbon atoms long.|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Bromine water is an orange solution, and we use it to test whether a hydrocarbon is unsaturated. Take ethene, which is a gas, and bubble it through this orange bromine water. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: What happens when ethene gas is bubbled through orange bromine water?|id=ex-q-1>> Ethene has a carbon-carbon double bond, so it reacts with bromine water in an addition reaction. The bromine adds straight across that double bond. <<WRITE_STEP:ethene (gas) + bromine water (orange) gives an addition reaction|id=ex-step-1-1>> The product is one-two-dibromoethane, which is colourless, so the orange colour disappears. <<WRITE_ANSWER:ethene + bromine water gives 1,2-dibromoethane (colourless) — the orange colour disappears|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We're asked to compare three compounds that all share the very same molecular formula, C four H eight. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Three compounds all have formula C4H8 but different structures. What are they?|id=ex-q-1>> So all three have formula C four H eight, but when we draw them out we find they have different structures and the double bond sits in different positions. That tells us straight away these are isomers of one another. <<WRITE_STEP:Same formula C4H8, different structures and double-bond positions -> isomers|id=ex-step-1>> And the answer is that the three isomers are but-one-ene, but-two-ene, and two-methylpropene, all members of the alkene family. <<WRITE_ANSWER:The three C4H8 isomers are but-1-ene, but-2-ene and 2-methylpropene|id=ex-ans-1>> <<FOCUS:ethane-single-bond>> A molecule with a double bond waiting to open is called unsaturated. Once it has grabbed its extra atoms and the doorway is shut, it is saturated, just like the lazy alkane next door. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:ethene-double-bond>> So that is the whole secret. The double bond costs an alkene one pair of hydrogens, giving the formula C-n-H-2-n, and that same double bond is the open doorway that makes alkenes far more reactive than alkanes.

questions.q_text: Explain why molecules like pentane, cyclohexane, and three-methyl pentane can all be different shapes even though they are all hydrocarbons.
questions.answer: All hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen atoms. The key feature is that carbon atoms can bond to other carbon atoms, forming the 'spine' or backbone of the molecule, with hydrogen atoms attached to those carbons. Because carbon can link to carbon in different arrangements, the backbone can take different shapes. In pentane, five carbons link in a straight chain. In cyclohexane, six carbons join end to end to form a closed ring. In three-methyl pentane, the main carbon chain has an extra carbon group branching off to the side. So even though the building blocks (carbon and hydrogen) are the same, the way the carbon atoms connect to each other produces straight chains, rings, or branched structures.

questions.q_text: You collect two fractions from petroleum. Fraction A is gasoline, made of small molecules. Fraction B is bitumen, made of very large molecules. Compare these two fractions in terms of boiling point, viscosity, volatility, and how easily they burn. Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer:
Step 1: Recall the golden rule — the larger the molecules in a hydrocarbon, the higher its boiling point, the less volatile it is, the less easily it flows (more viscous), and the less easily it burns.

Step 2: Fraction A (gasoline) has small molecules. Small molecules need little energy to escape, so gasoline has a LOW boiling point, is HIGHLY volatile (evaporates easily), is runny (low viscosity, flows easily), and burns very easily.

Step 3: Fraction B (bitumen) has very large molecules. Large molecules hold on tightly, so bitumen has a HIGH boiling point, is barely volatile, is very thick (high viscosity, flows poorly), and is very hard to burn — it barely lights at all.

Conclusion: Compared to bitumen, gasoline boils at a lower temperature, is more volatile, flows more easily, and ignites far more readily. This is exactly why gasoline is used as a fuel for cars while bitumen is used to surface roads.

questions.q_text: In a lab cracking experiment, the delivery tube ends under water. Explain what you must do the instant you stop heating, and why.
questions.answer: As soon as you stop heating, you must lift the delivery tube out of the water. When heating stops, the gas in the hot test tube cools and contracts, which reduces the pressure inside the tube. If the tube is still under the water, the lower pressure causes water to be sucked back up the delivery tube into the very hot test tube. The cold water hitting the hot glass would cause it to crack or shatter. Removing the tube from the water first prevents this 'suck-back' and keeps the apparatus safe.

questions.q_text: A refinery finds it has a large surplus of naphtha but a shortage of gasoline, and it also needs reactive molecules to make plastics. Explain how cracking solves both of these problems.
questions.answer: Cracking breaks large molecules into smaller ones, so it allows the refinery to make the best use of its petroleum. First, the surplus naphtha has carbon chains that are longer than needed. By cracking the naphtha, the long chains snap into shorter pieces that are the right size for gasoline (petrol), turning a surplus of one fraction into the fraction that is in short supply. Second, cracking always produces some short-chain molecules that contain a carbon-to-carbon double bond. This double bond makes the molecules reactive, and these reactive molecules are exactly what is needed as raw materials for making plastics. So a single process both balances the supply of fuels and provides reactive feedstock for plastics.

questions.q_text: Using the general formula for alkanes, work out the molecular formula of the alkane that has five carbon atoms, and state its name.
questions.answer: The general formula for alkanes is C-n-H-(two-n-plus-two), where n is the number of carbon atoms. Here n equals 5. First find the carbon part: there are 5 carbon atoms, so C-5. Next find the hydrogen part: two times n plus two equals two times 5 plus two, which is 10 plus 2, equals 12 hydrogen atoms. So the formula is C-5-H-12. The name uses pent- for five carbons and the -ane ending for an alkane, so the compound is pentane.

questions.q_text: An alkane molecule contains 6 carbon atoms. Using the general formula for alkanes, work out how many hydrogen atoms it has and write its molecular formula.
questions.answer: The general formula for alkanes is C-n-H-(two-n-plus-two). Here n equals 6. First find the number of hydrogens: two times n is two times 6, which is 12. Then add 2, giving 14 hydrogen atoms. So the molecule has 6 carbons and 14 hydrogens, and its molecular formula is C-six-H-fourteen.

questions.q_text: Butane and two-methylpropane both have the formula C-four-H-ten. Explain what name we give compounds like these, and predict which one has the higher boiling point and why.
questions.answer: Compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures are called isomers. Butane is a straight chain of four carbons, while two-methylpropane is branched. Branched molecules cannot pack as closely together because the branches hold the molecules apart, so the attraction between them is weaker and less energy is needed to separate them. Therefore the branched isomer, two-methylpropane, has the lower boiling point, and the straight-chain butane has the higher boiling point.

questions.q_text: A hydrocarbon is found to have three carbon atoms and six hydrogen atoms. Decide whether it could be an alkene, name it, and explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: Step 1: Check the hydrogen-to-carbon pattern for alkenes. In an alkene, the number of hydrogen atoms is always exactly twice the number of carbon atoms. Step 2: Here there are 3 carbons, so twice that is 6 hydrogens. The molecule has 6 hydrogens, so it fits the alkene pattern. Step 3: An alkene with 3 carbon atoms is called propene. Step 4: Therefore the molecule could be propene, an unsaturated hydrocarbon containing a carbon-to-carbon double bond, since it matches the alkene formula where hydrogens are double the carbons.

questions.q_text: Explain why ethanol made from plants is said to have less impact on carbon dioxide levels than fossil fuels, even though burning ethanol still releases carbon dioxide.
questions.answer: Step 1: When ethanol burns in oxygen it produces carbon dioxide and water, so it does release carbon dioxide into the air. Step 2: However, ethanol is made from plant material, and plants grow by taking in carbon dioxide from the atmosphere during photosynthesis. Step 3: So the carbon dioxide released when ethanol burns is roughly balanced by the carbon dioxide the plants soaked up while growing. Step 4: This makes the process much closer to carbon neutral. Step 5: Fossil fuels are different because they release carbon that was locked away underground millions of years ago, adding extra carbon dioxide to today's atmosphere that is not being reabsorbed in the same way. Therefore ethanol from plants has less overall impact on carbon dioxide levels.

questions.q_text: Ethanoic acid reacts with propanol in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid. Name the type of reaction, the catalyst's role, the organic product, and the other product formed.
questions.answer: Step 1: Identify the reactants — ethanoic acid (a carboxylic acid) and propanol (an alcohol). Step 2: When an acid reacts with an alcohol, an ester is formed. The ester is named from the alcohol part first then the acid part: the propanol gives 'propyl' and the ethanoic acid gives 'ethanoate', so the ester is propyl ethanoate. Step 3: The concentrated sulfuric acid acts as a catalyst, speeding up the reaction without being used up. Step 4: Because two molecules join together and a small water molecule is lost, this is a condensation reaction, and it is reversible. So the products are propyl ethanoate plus water.

questions.q_text: Ethanoic acid is reacted with sodium hydroxide. Identify what kind of reaction this is and name the products formed.
questions.answer: Step 1: Ethanoic acid is an acid and sodium hydroxide is a base (an alkali). Step 2: An acid reacting with a base is a neutralisation reaction, which always produces a salt plus water. Step 3: The salt is formed from the sodium of the hydroxide and the ethanoate from the acid, giving sodium ethanoate. Step 4: Therefore the products are sodium ethanoate and water.

questions.q_text: Explain why ethene fits the formula CnH2n but ethane does not, and state what happens to ethene's classification when it adds hydrogen across its double bond.
questions.answer: Ethene has 2 carbon atoms. Using the alkene general formula CnH2n with n equal to 2 gives 2 times 2, which is 4 hydrogen atoms, so ethene is C2H4 and fits the formula. Ethane has 2 carbons but is saturated with only single bonds, so it has 6 hydrogen atoms (C2H6); 2 times 2 would only be 4, so ethane does not fit CnH2n. When ethene adds hydrogen across its double bond, the double bond opens and two extra hydrogen atoms are added, turning C2H4 into C2H6. This converts the unsaturated alkene into a saturated alkane (ethane).

questions.q_text: Three different molecules all share the formula C4H8. Explain how molecules with the same formula can be different compounds, and what the numbers in names like but-1-ene and but-2-ene tell us.
questions.answer: Molecules with the same formula but different structures are called isomers. Even though all three have 4 carbons and 8 hydrogens (matching CnH2n for an alkene), the atoms can be arranged differently: the carbon chain may branch in different ways, or the carbon-to-carbon double bond may sit in a different position along the chain. The numbers in the names show exactly where the double bond is located: but-1-ene has the double bond starting at the first carbon, while but-2-ene has it starting at the second carbon. So the number pinpoints the double bond's position, distinguishing one isomer from another.
